candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Secondary Aluminum Production

criteria.criterion: If your establishment is a secondary aluminum production facility as defined in § 63.1503, then the requirements of this subpart apply to the owner or operator.

If the secondary aluminum production facility is a major source of HAPs, then each thermal chip dryer at that facility is an affected source subject to the subpart's requirements (including the THC and D/F emission standards listed for thermal chip dryers).

If the secondary aluminum production facility is an area source of HAPs, then the dioxin/furan (D/F) requirements of this subpart apply to each thermal chip dryer (even though the THC major-source limits apply only to major sources).

If the unit processes painted or coated scrap (i.e., is not limited to unpainted/uncoated chips and is used primarily to remove paint/lacquer/organic coatings), then it does not meet the regulatory definition of 'thermal chip dryer' and instead may be a scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln subject to the separate affected-source listing and requirements.
citations: 40 CFR 63.1503 (definition of thermal chip dryer and scrap dryer/delacquering kiln/decoating kiln)

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If a relevant subpart standard (e.g., subpart RRR) requires a performance test for an affected source or emission unit, then the owner/operator must comply with the performance testing requirements in § 63.7 (including notification timings and the general 180‑day test timing provisions unless an approved extension/waiver applies).

If the relevant standard requires continuous monitoring systems or other CMS, then the owner/operator must comply with the monitoring operation, QA/QC, data reduction, and recordkeeping requirements in § 63.8 for those systems.

checklist: Is your facility a 'secondary aluminum production facility' as defined in 40 CFR 63.1503 (i.e., does the establishment perform scrap shredding, scrap drying/delacquering/decoating, thermal chip drying, furnace operations, dross recovery, in-line fluxing, or dross cooling)?
Is the facility a major source of HAPs (≥10 tons/year of any single listed HAP or ≥25 tons/year of combined HAPs) or an area source? (determine potential to emit per 40 CFR 63.2)

What exact feedstock will the dryer process: only unpainted/uncoated aluminum chips (meeting the 'chips' definition) or shredded scrap that contains paint/coatings? (document paint/coating presence, % by weight or typical contamination levels)

What is the primary purpose of the unit: evaporate oil/oil-water from unpainted chips (thermal chip dryer definition) or remove paint/lacquer/organic coatings (scrap dryer/delacquering/decoating kiln)?

Will the dryer be operated with only unpainted chips (if claiming it is a thermal chip dryer), and can you certify/record the type of materials charged for each operating cycle as required? (see operational/monitoring requirements)

Will you install control equipment (e.g., afterburner, fabric filter, lime injection) and, if so, what devices and their design parameters (afterburner design residence time, operating temperature, fabric filter type)?

Do you plan to conduct performance testing for THC and D/F at the outlet of the control device while processing only unpainted chips (per § 63.1512(b))? If so, can you meet the notification and scheduling requirements in § 63.7?

If you assert that low operating temperature prevents formation of VOCs or D/F, can you document that position with engineering data — note the regulatory applicability tests are based on facility/type of unit and feedstock definitions, not operating temperature, per the cited provisions.

If the facility is an aluminum die casting, foundry, or extrusion facility, does it meet the conditions in § 63.1503(f) (e.g., only melting clean charge, and whether operating a thermal chip dryer makes the facility subject to the subpart)?

Are you prepared to assemble an OM&M plan and site-specific monitoring plan (if applicable) documenting monitored parameters, feed/charge measurement method, and work practices as required by § 63.1510 and to keep the required records and certifications for 6‑month reporting periods?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key EPA reasons are captured: the answer identifies that drying painted scrap classifies the unit as a scrap dryer/delacquering/decoating kiln under §63.1503 (not a thermal chip dryer), it notes that operating temperature (660°F) does not by itself eliminate HAP applicability and must be documented, and it addresses the major‑source vs area‑source requirements for the unit."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants From Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric Utility Steam Generating Units

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a coal-fired EGU or an oil-fired EGU as defined in 40 CFR 63.10042, then you are subject to this subpart.
If your unit meets the definition of a natural gas-fired EGU in 40 CFR 63.10042, then your unit is not subject to this subpart.

If your unit is capable of combusting more than 25 MW of coal or oil but did not fire sufficient coal or oil to meet the coal- or oil-fired EGU fuel-use thresholds in 40 CFR 63.10042, then your unit is not subject to this subpart.

If you are a coal-fired, liquid oil-fired, or solid oil-derived fuel-fired EGU, then the emission limits and operating limits of this subpart apply at all times except during periods of startup and shutdown, and during startup or shutdown you must meet the work practice requirements in Table 3 to this subpart.

If the boiler is fired after a shutdown event for any purpose, then that firing is a 'startup' under paragraph (1) of the definition of 'startup' and the startup period ends when any steam from the boiler is used to generate electricity for sale or for any other purpose (including on-site use).

If you elect (only allowed before January 2, 2025) to rely on paragraph (2) of the 'startup' definition, then 'startup' begins when fuel is first fired to produce electricity or useful thermal energy (including on-site steam) and ends 4 hours after the unit generates electricity or makes useful thermal energy (whichever is earlier); after January 2, 2025 you may not rely on paragraph (2).

If you choose to rely on paragraph (2) of the 'startup' definition (only allowed before January 2, 2025), then during each period of startup you must record the date/time clean fuels begin, the quantity and heat input of clean fuel each hour of startup, the gross output each hour of startup, the date/time non-clean fuel combustion begins, and the date/time clean fuel combustion ends as required in 40 CFR 63.10020(e)(1).

If your unit qualifies as a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU as defined in 40 CFR 63.10042 (annual capacity factor when burning oil < 8 percent over the specified period), then your unit is not subject to the emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 but must comply with the tune-up work practice requirements in Table 3.

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If you are subject to an applicable Part 63 standard, then the Subpart A General Provisions apply to that standard, including the definitions in § 63.2 and the performance testing and monitoring requirements in §§ 63.7 and 63.8.

If performance testing is required by a relevant standard, then you must perform the tests within the timeframes and with the notifications, site-specific test plan, and QA program required by 40 CFR 63.7 (including providing at least 60 days' notice and testing under representative conditions; startup/shutdown are not representative conditions).

If a continuous monitoring system (CMS) is required by the relevant standard, then you must install, operate, quality-assure, and maintain the CMS consistent with the requirements and out-of-control/QA provisions in 40 CFR 63.8.

checklist: Confirm whether the unit is an 'electric utility steam generating unit (EGU)' that serves a generator producing electricity for sale and whether it meets the coal-fired or oil-fired EGU fuel-use thresholds in 40 CFR 63.10042 (review fuel mix and percent heat input for the prior applicable years).
Verify the unit's nameplate/maximum sustainable electrical output (MW) and whether it is capable of combusting >25 MW of coal or oil (per 40 CFR 63.10042 and 63.9983(c)).
Determine whether the specific firing event is after a shutdown (i.e., a restart after a period when no fuel was being fired) — if so, document that it is a post-shutdown firing.

Determine the purpose of the firing: is the steam produced being used for any purpose (including on-site uses such as heating fuel tanks) and, if so, record the date/time steam first goes into service (because under 40 CFR 63.10042(1) startup ends when steam is used for any purpose).

If you intend to treat the event as 'startup' under paragraph (2) of the definition, confirm whether that reliance is allowed for the event date (paragraph (2) was only available prior to January 2, 2025 per 40 CFR 63.10000(m)); if relying on paragraph (2), prepare to record the specific startup data fields required by 40 CFR 63.10020(e).

Check whether the unit qualifies as a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU (annual oil capacity factor < 8% per 40 CFR 63.10042) which affects whether emission limits or only tune-up/work practices apply.

Confirm current monitoring and control configuration: which CEMS/CPMS/sorbent trap systems are installed and operable, and ensure CMS operation and data collection during the firing per 40 CFR 63.10000(d), 63.10020(b), and 63.10007(f).

Verify applicable startup/shutdown work practice obligations in Table 3 to Subpart UUUUU (review Table 3 requirements and ensure procedures and recordkeeping to meet those work practices are in place).

If you plan to include the event as part of a compliance demonstration or LEE testing, verify how startup/shutdown hours are treated for your chosen compliance method (CEMS 30- or 90-boiler operating day averages, sorbent traps, PM CPMS, or performance stack tests) per 40 CFR 63.10007, 63.10005, and 63.10011.

Document and retain records showing timing of fuel firing, fuel types and quantities, start/stop times, gross output (MW), and any CMS data or parameter logs for the event to support applicability and startup characterization under the cited provisions.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key reasons are captured: the Answer cites 40 CFR 63.10042(1) and states that startup ends when steam is used for any purpose (including on‑site auxiliary steam) and the checklist repeats that auxiliary steam use ends startup — matching the EPA note's rationale."}

candidates.title: Subpart UUUUU

criteria.criterion: If the unit is a fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating unit (an EGU: capable of producing more than 25 MWe, serving a generator that produces electricity for sale) then the unit is potentially subject to Subpart UUUUU.

If the EGU burns oil for more than 10.0 percent of the average annual heat input during the 3 previous calendar years (or for more than 15.0 percent of the annual heat input during any one of those calendar years) then it meets the definition of an oil-fired EGU and is in the oil-fired EGU subcategories.

If the annual capacity factor for the unit when burning oil (annual heat input from oil divided by maximum hourly heat input regardless of fuel × 8,760) is less than 8 percent averaged over a 24-month contiguous block beginning the first of the month after the applicable compliance date, then the unit meets the definition of a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU.

If the unit qualifies as a limited-use liquid oil-fired EGU as defined in §63.10042, then it is not subject to the emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 of this subpart but must comply with the performance tune-up work practice requirements in Table 3 to this subpart.
If the unit meets the definition of a natural gas-fired EGU in §63.10042, then it is not subject to Subpart UUUUU.

If the unit has the capability of combusting more than 25 MW of coal or oil but did not fire sufficient coal or oil to meet the oil-fired or coal-fired EGU definitions (based on the multi-year percent heat-input tests in §63.10042), then it is not subject to this subpart.

candidates.title: Subpart DDDDD

criteria.criterion: If the boiler is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) covered by Subpart UUUUU then it is not subject to Subpart DDDDD.
If the boiler is a natural gas-fired EGU as defined in Subpart UUUUU and it fires at least 85 percent natural gas on an annual heat input basis, then it is not subject to Subpart DDDDD.

If the unit otherwise qualifies as a limited-use boiler or process heater under Subpart DDDDD, then it is not subject to the emission limits in Tables 1 and 2 of that subpart but must complete the tune-up every 5 years specified in §63.7540.

candidates.title: Subpart A

criteria.criterion: If the unit is subject to a relevant standard established under part 63 (e.g., Subpart UUUUU), then the General Provisions in Subpart A apply to that unit (definitions, monitoring, testing, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements).

If the relevant standard or subpart requires performance testing, then the owner or operator must perform the required performance tests within 180 days of the compliance date (unless another provision applies or a waiver/extension is obtained).

If the relevant standard requires continuous monitoring systems (CMS), CEMS, or CPMS to demonstrate compliance, then those systems and their operation, QA/QC, and reporting are subject to the requirements of §63.8.

checklist: Confirm whether Unit 1 is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU): does it serve a generator that produces electricity for sale and is it capable of producing >25 MWe? (definition in 40 CFR 63.10042).

Determine the unit's maximum hourly heat input (MMBtu/hr) used in the capacity-factor calculation (nameplate or design maximum); verify the provided 4,286 MMBtu/hr and the unit's maximum sustainable electrical output (if available).

Calculate annual heat input from oil (MMBtu/year) for the applicable 24-month block: sum all heat input from No.2 and No.4 fuel oil in each 12-month period, then compute capacity factor for oil = (annual heat input from oil) / (maximum hourly heat input × 8,760) and average per the required 24-month contiguous block.
Verify whether the oil capacity factor (as calculated above) is less than 8% averaged over the required 24-month block to meet the limited-use liquid oil-fired definition in 40 CFR 63.10042.

Determine the fraction of the unit's annual heat input from oil, natural gas, and any coal or other fuels for the 3 previous calendar years (or projected first 3 years if applicable) to test the oil-fired vs natural gas-fired EGU definitions (oil-fired: >10% average over 3 years or >15% in any one year; natural-gas-fired criteria in 40 CFR 63.10042).

Document fuel types and properties: confirm No.2 is distillate oil and No.4 is residual oil, and record any 'clean fuel' usage (distillate oil and natural gas are listed as clean fuels in 40 CFR 63.10042) because some monitoring/testing alternatives reference clean fuels.
Check whether the unit sells electricity or provides only on-site steam (to determine EGU status vs other boiler/process heater categories).
Verify the applicable compliance date and the 24-month averaging window start (see §63.9984 referenced in the definitions) to know which months to include in the capacity-factor averaging period.
Check recent and historical operating hours and fuel consumption records (daily/monthly fuel use and heat input) to produce the required percent-heat-input and capacity-factor calculations.

Check whether there is a federally enforceable permit limit (e.g., Title V) that constrains annual capacity factor or fuel use (records required for limited-use boilers/process heaters per 40 CFR 63.7555(a)(3) and related subparts).
If claiming non-applicability under Subpart DDDDD, verify that the unit is covered by Subpart UUUUU or that it fires ≥85% natural gas on an annual heat input basis per 40 CFR 63.7491(a).

If you determine the unit may be a limited-use unit, prepare to document and retain the calculations and supporting fuel/use records showing the 24-month average capacity factor when burning oil and all related records required by the applicable subpart (fuel use, fuel analyses if used, and permit limits).

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"EPA’s reasons — that the unit is an oil-fired EGU per §63.10042 and that it qualifies as the limited-use liquid oil-fired subcategory (see §63.9990(b)(3)/§63.10042 criteria) — are explicitly represented in the submitted criteria (oil-fired definition and the <8% oil capacity-factor limited‑use test), so all key reasons are captured."}

candidates.title: General Provisions (definitions, performance testing, monitoring)

criteria.criterion: If your facility or collection of equipment meets the definition of an 'affected source' under this part, then the general provisions in subpart A (definitions and applicability principles) apply to determine and implement applicability and compliance
If a relevant NESHAP requires performance testing for your affected source, then you must comply with the performance testing requirements in § 63.7
If a relevant NESHAP requires continuous monitoring or other CMS for demonstrating compliance, then you must comply with the monitoring requirements in § 63.8

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Miscellaneous Coating Manufacturing Operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations that (1) are located at or are part of a major source of HAP, (2) manufacture 'coatings' as defined in § 63.8105, (3) process/use/produce HAP, and (4) are not part of an affected source under another subpart, then you are subject to subpart HHHHH

If the material you produce is excluded from the definition of 'coating' because a formulation component is synthesized by chemical reaction or separation activity and then transferred to another vessel where it is formulated and the synthesized/separated component is not stored prior to formulation, then that material is not a 'coating' for purposes of subpart HHHHH

If equipment is used both for miscellaneous coating manufacturing and is part of a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU) and you meet the process unit group (PUG) and primary-product criteria and comply with subpart FFFF as specified, then complying with subpart FFFF under the conditions in § 63.8090(c) can be deemed to satisfy subpart HHHHH requirements for that equipment

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing Process Units (MCPU)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) located at or part of a major source and the MCPU (1) produces materials described in § 63.2435(b)(1) (SIC/NAICS organic chemicals or specified categories), (2) processes, uses, or generates organic HAP or hydrogen halide and halogen HAP, and (3) is not an affected source or part of an affected source under another subpart, then you are subject to subpart FFFF

If the operation is an 'affiliated operation' located at an affected source that is subject to certain surface-coating subparts (examples listed) and is limited to activities such as mixing or dissolving of coating ingredients, then that affiliated operation is excluded from subpart FFFF

If the step in question is a 'unit operation' (e.g., filtration, centrifuging, decanting) that is a processing step used to prepare reactants, separate or purify products, or otherwise function as part of a manufacturing process, then that separation/filtration activity can be part of an MCPU and thus may bring the equipment/step within subpart FFFF

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined)? (determine major source status)
Does the operation 'manufacture coatings' as defined in 40 CFR 63.8105 (i.e., is the product intended as a coating produced by blending/mixing/formulation)?

Does any part of the coating formulation result from a synthesis by chemical reaction or from a separation activity that produces a component which is then transferred (without storage) to a formulation vessel (i.e., does your filtering step create a separated component that is transferred and not stored)?

Describe the filtration step in detail: equipment used, purpose (remove gels/lumps vs. separate a component), whether material removed is collected as a separate product/stream, and whether the filtered stream is recycled, stored, or transferred to another vessel before formulation
Is the filtration operation described as a 'unit operation' within a process that prepares/recovers/separates/purifies materials (e.g., is filtration listed among process equipment for your unit)?
What are the NAICS/SIC codes and the chemical nature of the materials produced (do they fall under the organic-chemical categories in § 63.2435(b)(1)/(2))?

Are the coating-manufacturing vessels/equipment assigned to a Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing Process Unit (MCPU) or to miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations (i.e., could equipment be part of a process unit group / PUG)?
Does the operation process, use, or produce HAP? List HAPs used/generated and estimated emissions or potential to emit.
Is any portion of the operation already part of an affected source under another NESHAP subpart (e.g., listed subparts or other chemical NESHAP)?
If equipment is shared between coating manufacture and chemical manufacturing, can you meet the PUG and primary-product criteria and elect compliance with subpart FFFF as allowed by § 63.8090(c)?

judge_text: {"score":1,"reason":"Some of the EPA Notes’ factors appear in the criteria (the coating-definition/separation-exclusion language and the FFFF affiliation/exclusion citations and unit-operation language are cited), but the answer does not capture the EPA’s central determination that a final filtration of a finished coating is not a “separation activity” under §63.8105 (and thus HHHHH applies and FFFF is excluded under §63.2435(b)(3))."}

candidates.title: Petroleum refinery NESHAP (Subpart CC)

criteria.criterion: If the combustion device lacks an enclosed combustion chamber and uses an uncontrolled volume of ambient air to burn gases, then it is a flare under this subpart.

If the vapor control device is an enclosed combustion device (for example, an incinerator, boiler, or process heater with an enclosed combustion chamber), then it is not a flare and is treated as a control device rather than a flare for the purposes of the refinery NESHAP.

If the tank/loader/vehicle loading operation is a gasoline loading rack that is a Group 1 gasoline loading rack and a flare is used as the control device for that loading rack, then the flare must meet the requirements of § 63.670.

If a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent (including a gasoline loading rack vent that meets Group 1 criteria) uses a combustion device to comply with § 63.643(a), then the monitoring provisions in § 63.644 apply and the specific monitoring requirement depends on the type of combustion device used (e.g., incinerator vs flare vs boiler/process heater).

If vent streams are routed to a refinery fuel gas system or other process rather than directly to the combustor, then those vent points are not treated as miscellaneous process vents for this subpart, but any flares receiving gas from the fuel gas system (on and after January 30, 2019) are required to meet § 63.670.

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a control or flare is subject to a subpart standard that requires performance testing or continuous monitoring, then the general provisions on performance testing (required timing, test plans, QA) in § 63.7 apply to that testing.

If a control device or flare is subject to continuous monitoring or continuous parameter monitoring under a relevant subpart standard, then the general CMS/monitoring operation, QA, out-of-control and data-reduction rules in § 63.8 apply.

If an affected unit is subject to a relevant standard under this part, then the definitions and applicability concepts in § 63.2 (e.g., affected source, monitoring definitions) apply in interpreting which monitoring and testing duties are triggered.

checklist: Is the truck loading rack at Plant 2 a 'gasoline loading rack' (SIC 2911) and, if so, does it meet the Group 1 criteria (e.g., throughput and vapor characteristics) in § 63.641/§ 63.650?

Is the vapor control unit an enclosed combustion chamber (incinerator, enclosed thermal oxidizer, boiler, or process heater) or an open flare (i.e., lacks an enclosed combustion chamber and burns with uncontrolled ambient air)?
Do piping/ducting diagrams show whether the truck loading rack vapors are routed directly to the combustor (control device) or first routed to a fuel gas system or other process?

Is the combustor design such that ambient air is the oxidant (uncontrolled entrainment) versus a contained combustion chamber with forced/controlled combustion and auxiliary fuel (manufacturer drawings, spec sheet)?

Is the combustor being used to meet the Group 1 miscellaneous process vent or gasoline loading rack control requirement under § 63.643/§ 63.650 (i.e., is it functioning as the required control device for HAP reduction)?

If the device could be a flare, does it have pilot flame monitoring, flow/composition monitors, and other features consistent with § 63.670/§ 63.671 (check presence/absence of enclosed chamber, assist steam/air design, continuous monitors, and surveillance capability)?

Is the Plant 2 loading rack and combustor located on the same contiguous plant site under common control as the refinery (plant-site/common-control determination per § 63.641 'plant site' and § 63.640)?

Are there records or process knowledge showing whether the vent stream composition or net heating value is consistent or variable (this affects applicability of continuous composition/NHV monitoring or possible exemptions per § 63.670(j))?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key EPA reasons are reflected: the answer cites the §63.641 distinction (enclosed combustor vs flare), recognizes that §63.670/63.671 apply to flares (and thus would not apply if §63.641 is not met), and includes the obligation to test and set/monitor operating parameters via §63.643/§63.644 and the general provisions (§63.7/§63.8) to demonstrate compliance with Subpart CC limits."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Paper and Other Web Coating Operations

criteria.criterion: If a coating line applies a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating material across the entire width or a portion of the width of a continuous flexible substrate that is fed from an unwind/feed station and collected at a rewind or cutting station with any associated curing/drying equipment between the feed and rewind, then that line meets the Subpart JJJJ definition of a 'web coating line' and is the type of emission source addressed by this subpart.

If your facility is a major source of HAP (as defined in the General Provisions) and operates one or more web coating lines, then the provisions of Subpart JJJJ apply to the facility's web coating operations.

If the coating operation uses discrete sheets (not a continuous flexible substrate that can be wound/unwound as rolls), then that operation does not meet the Subpart JJJJ definition of 'web' and is not a 'web coating line' for this subpart.

If a web coating line is covered by another listed subpart (for example, is stand-alone under subpart KK, or subject to subparts EE, SSSS, OOOO, or is defined as research/laboratory equipment), then that web coating line is excluded from the affected source under Subpart JJJJ and is not part of Subpart JJJJ's affected source.

If a single web coating line coats more than one type of substrate (e.g., paper and fabric), then the subpart that applies may be determined by the predominant activity (90 percent by mass of substrate coated during the compliance period) as described in this subpart.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Refractory Products Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plant site that manufactures refractory products (products used as linings for high-temperature process units and meeting the 'refractory product' definition) and the plant site is a major source of HAP, then the facility is subject to Subpart SSSSS.

If the finished product is a 'refractory product' — i.e., a nonmetallic material containing less than 50 percent carbon by weight and having chemical and physical properties for use in environments above 538 °C (1000 °F) — then that finished product meets the Subpart SSSSS definition of refractory product.

If the refractory product is produced using substances that are organic HAP (for example resin-bonded or pitch-bonded processes, or products that release or contain organic HAP during production), then the product is a 'refractory product that uses organic HAP' as defined in this subpart and the associated provisions for such products apply.

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If an emission standard in this part (such as Subpart JJJJ or Subpart SSSSS) applies to an affected source, then Subpart A's definitions, testing, monitoring, and related general provisions are also applicable to that affected source.

If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the owner or operator must perform the required performance tests within the deadlines and subject to the procedures in § 63.7 (including notification, site-specific test plans, QA, and reporting) unless a waiver or extension is granted.

If continuous monitoring, parametric monitoring, or other CMS/CPMS is required by a relevant standard or subpart, then the monitoring design, operation, QA/QC, performance-evaluation, data reduction, and out-of-control handling requirements in § 63.8 apply.

checklist: Is the substrate on the roll-fed mica line a continuous flexible web (capable of being wound/unwound as a roll) rather than discrete sheets?

On the roll-fed line, is a continuous layer of liquid or semi-liquid coating applied across the width (or part of the width) of that continuous substrate between an unwind/feed station and a rewind or cutting station, and is there curing/drying equipment in that path?
On the sheet-handled line, are individual discrete sheets coated (no unwind/feed and rewind/cutting) rather than processed as a continuous web?

Does any coating operation deposit coating material by printing or other processes that would place it under another subpart (e.g., printing presses/subpart KK, textile coating/subpart OOOO, metal coil/subpart SSSS)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP)?
Do the coatings or binders used on either line contain organic HAP (check formulation data, Method 311/24 results, or manufacturer data)?

For mixed-substrate lines: what fraction (mass) of substrate coated is paper/web versus other substrates (calculate percent mass coated over a representative period, e.g., one year) to evaluate the 90% predominant-activity rule?
For the finished mica insulation products: are they intended for use in high-temperature service (exposure above 538 °C / 1000 °F)?
For the finished mica products: what is the total carbon content (by weight) of the finished product — is it less than 50% carbon by weight?

Are the finished products manufactured via refractory-style operations (raw-material processing, mixing with binders/additives, forming, drying/curing, firing) or instead manufactured as flexible mica paper products without refractory firing?

Do the product formulations or process steps use organic HAP-containing resins, pitch, or other organic HAPs (e.g., phenolic resins, pitch impregnation, methanol/ethylene glycol-containing materials)?

If considering compliance obligations: do you have any control devices, solvent recovery units, or oxidizers on the coating exhaust streams (needed to determine monitoring and test requirements under JJJJ and Subpart A)?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The Answer includes the web-coating definition and the discrete-sheet exclusion (40 CFR 63.3300/63.3310) explaining why the roll‑fed line is a web subject to JJJJ and the sheet line is not, and it includes the refractory-product definition/criteria (40 CFR 63.9824) and related checklist items (temperature use, % carbon, production methods, organic HAPs) supporting why the mica products are not subject to Subpart SSSSS. All key reasons from the EPA Notes are present."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Natural Gas Transmission and Storage (glycol dehydration units)

criteria.criterion: If the facility is a natural gas transmission and storage facility that is a major source of HAP, then Subpart HHH applies to glycol dehydration units at the facility.

If a glycol dehydration unit process vent is routed to an enclosed combustion device (e.g., boiler or process heater) as the control device, then the vent stream must be introduced into the flame zone and the control-device provisions of this subpart apply.
citations: 40 CFR 63.1271 (definitions of control device and process heater)

criteria.criterion: If the glycol dehydration unit process vent is routed to a flare through a closed-vent system that meets the subpart's closed-vent and flare requirements, then the subpart allows using a flare as the control device for the process vent.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters (Boiler and Process Heater MACT)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater located at or part of a major source of HAP, then Subpart DDDDD applies to that boiler or process heater, except as excluded in § 63.7491.

If the boiler or process heater is part of an affected source that is subject to another part 63 subpart (i.e., 'part of the affected source' regulated under another subpart), then that boiler or process heater is not subject to Subpart DDDDD.

If the boiler or process heater is used as a control device to comply with another subpart and at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years is provided by regulated gas streams that are subject to another standard, then it is not subject to Subpart DDDDD.

candidates.title: General Provisions (performance testing, monitoring, and definitions)

criteria.criterion: If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the owner or operator must perform performance tests in accordance with § 63.7.
If a relevant standard requires a continuous monitoring system or other CMS, then the monitoring requirements of § 63.8 apply to that CMS.

If the facility or equipment meets the definitions (for example, 'major source' or terms used in relevant subparts), then the definitions and terms in § 63.2 govern applicability and related determinations.

checklist: Confirm whether the facility is a major source of HAP (calculate potential/actual emissions per the major source definition and Subpart HHH § 63.1270/§ 63.2).
Verify whether the subject unit is the glycol dehydration unit reboiler (i.e., the reboiler that regenerates glycol) or a separate boiler/process heater.

Determine whether the dehydration unit process vent (still vent/flash tank vent) is routed to the reboiler flame zone, to a flare, to a fuel gas system, or to another control device (i.e., is the reboiler being used as the control device for the process vent?).
If the reboiler receives any process vent streams, document how the vent stream is introduced (into the flame zone, with the primary fuel, as a secondary fuel, or not introduced into the flame zone).

Establish the primary purpose of the reboiler burner: is it primarily transferring heat to a process fluid (glycol) (process heater definition) or primarily generating steam (boiler) (see Subpart HHH process heater/boiler definitions)?
Determine the fuels burned in the reboiler (field gas only, vent gas mixed with fuel, hazardous waste, etc.) and whether any vent stream is injected into the flame or combusted in that unit.

If claiming an exemption from Subpart DDDDD as a control-device exemption, calculate the fraction of average annual heat input from regulated gas streams subject to another standard to confirm whether the ≥50% criterion applies (per 40 CFR 63.7491(i)).

Document whether the glycol dehydration unit process vent is controlled via a closed-vent system to a control device and whether that closed-vent system meets the 'no detectable emissions' and bypass requirements in 40 CFR 63.1281(c).

Gather records and operating information needed for any required performance testing or monitoring (site-specific test plans, CPMS/CEMS design and QA procedures, pilot presence monitoring, flame/visible emissions data) in case Subpart HHH or Subpart A testing/monitoring rules apply.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"All key reasons are captured: the answer identifies that Subpart HHH governs the glycol still/flash vents and addresses whether vents are routed to a flare vs introduced into a combustion device, and it also includes Subpart DDDDD applicability/exclusions (including the 'part of affected source' and ≥50% control-device exemption) and checklist items to determine whether the reboiler is a process heater, what fuel it burns (i.e., not regulated by another subpart), and whether its exhaust is an uncontrolled stack."}

candidates.title: Area Source Standards for Electric Arc Furnace Steelmaking Facilities

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking facility that is an area source of hazardous air pollutant emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.
If the EAF steelmaking facility is located at a steel foundry (i.e., an EAF at a steel foundry), then the EAF steelmaking facility is excluded from this subpart and is not subject to it.
If your facility is a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), then this subpart does not apply to you.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Iron and Steel Foundries (Area Sources)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an iron and steel foundry that is an area source of hazardous air pollutant emissions, then you are subject to this subpart.

If your facility melts scrap, ingot, and/or other forms of iron and/or steel and pours the resulting molten metal into molds to produce final or near-final shape products for introduction into commerce, then your facility meets the definition of an 'iron and steel foundry' for purposes of this subpart.

If your operations do not include pouring molten metal into molds to produce final or near-final shape products (for example, if molten metal is converted into shot or grit by water atomization rather than poured into molds), then those operations do not meet the definition of an 'iron and steel foundry' for this subpart and are not subject to the foundry standards on that basis.

If your iron and steel foundry is an existing or new affected source you must determine classification (small versus large) based on metal melt production or capacity as specified, because applicability of some requirements depends on that classification.
If your facility is a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7), then this subpart does not apply to you.

candidates.title: Iron and Steel Foundries: Major Source Standards (Subpart EEEEE)

criteria.criterion: If your iron and steel foundry becomes a major source as defined in 40 CFR 63.2, then you must meet the requirements of 40 CFR part 63, subpart EEEEE.

If you operate an iron and steel foundry, this subpart (EEEEE) covers emissions from metal melting furnaces, scrap preheaters, pouring areas and stations, automated conveyor and pallet cooling lines, automated shakeout lines, mold and core making lines, and fugitive emissions from foundry operations.

candidates.title: General Provisions (Definitions, Performance Testing, and Monitoring)

criteria.criterion: If you are determining applicability under any relevant subpart, the definitions and general provisions in 40 CFR part 63 (including § 63.2) apply to interpret terms used in those subparts.

If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the performance testing requirements in § 63.7 apply, including timing (generally within 180 days of the compliance date) and site-specific test plan procedures.

If a relevant standard requires a continuous monitoring system (CMS) or other monitoring, then the monitoring requirements in § 63.8 apply (installation, operation, quality assurance, out-of-control procedures, and data reduction).

checklist: Does the facility operate an electric arc furnace (EAF) that produces molten steel? (Yes/No)
Are the EAF operations part of a steel foundry (i.e., is molten metal poured into molds on-site to produce final or near-final shape products for sale)?
Does the facility convert molten metal into shot, grit, or similar products by water atomization rather than pouring molten metal into molds?
Are the products produced 'final or near-final shape products for introduction into commerce' (commercial castings) or non-commercial/R&D items?
Is the facility an area source or a major source of HAPs (potential-to-emit ≥ 10 tpy of a single HAP or ≥ 25 tpy combined HAPs)?

For foundry evaluation: what was the facility's annual metal melt production for calendar year 2008 (existing) or annual metal melt capacity at startup (new)? (to classify small vs large foundry per 40 CFR 63.10880(f),(g))
For EAF steelmaking subpart timing: was construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced on or before September 20, 2007 (existing) or after (new)?
For foundry subpart timing: was construction or reconstruction of the affected source commenced before September 17, 2007 (existing) or on/after that date (new)?
Is the operation a research and development facility as defined in CAA section 112(c)(7)?
If metal is poured into molds, document the pouring, mold/core making, and shakeout operations (to confirm foundry operations per 40 CFR 63.10906 and 63.7682(b)).
If relying on EAF steelmaking subpart exclusion because of foundry location, document whether the EAF is 'at a steel foundry' and whether the facility meets the foundry definition in 40 CFR 63.10906.

If uncertainty exists, prepare records of process descriptions, flow diagrams, product descriptions (atomized shot/grit vs. poured castings), and annual metal melt production to support the applicability determination.

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"Yes. The EPA’s key rationale—that absence of pouring molten metal into molds means the operation does not meet the 40 CFR 63.10906 foundry definition (so subpart ZZZZZ/63.10880 does not apply) and therefore the facility remains subject to the EAF area source subpart YYYYY—is explicitly captured in the submitted criteria (ZZZZZ criterion stating atomization instead of pouring does not meet the foundry definition, plus YYYYY criteria covering EAF applicability and the foundry-location exclusion). (The EPA note also mentioned NSPS AAa, which the submission did not list, but the determinative definitional reason and EAF applicability are present.)"}

candidates.title: General Provisions (definitions, performance testing, and monitoring requirements)

criteria.criterion: if an affected source is subject to a relevant standard under part 63 then the definitions and general provisions of Subpart A (including applicability and definitions such as 'area source' and 'affected source') apply to that source

if a relevant standard requires performance testing then the performance testing requirements in §63.7 apply (including timing: perform tests within 180 days of the compliance date unless waived or extended, and the 60-day notice requirement for tests)

if a relevant standard requires a continuous monitoring system (CMS) or other monitoring then the monitoring design, operation, quality assurance, performance evaluation, data reduction, and reporting requirements in §63.8 apply

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers (Area Source Rule)

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler that is located at or is part of an area source of hazardous air pollutants then the boiler is subject to Subpart JJJJJJ except as provided in §63.11195

if the boiler meets the subpart's definition of a gas-fired boiler (burns gaseous fuels and burns liquid fuel only during periods of gas curtailment, supply interruption, startups, or for periodic testing/maintenance/operator training with such liquid-fuel use not exceeding the combined total of 48 hours during any calendar year) then the boiler is not subject to Subpart JJJJJJ

if the boiler is specifically listed as, or included in the definition of, an affected source in another standard under part 63 (or listed as affected under section 129 standards, or is covered by subpart EEE or a 3005 SWDA permit) then the boiler is not subject to Subpart JJJJJJ
if the boiler is an electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) as defined in §63.11237 then the boiler is not subject to Subpart JJJJJJ

if the boiler qualifies as a limited-use boiler (has a federally enforceable annual capacity factor of no more than 10 percent) then it is subject to the tune-up schedule and some management-practice provisions but is not subject to the emission limits and some operating limits in Subpart JJJJJJ

checklist: Is the facility an area source of HAPs (i.e., not a major source under part 63 definitions)? (see 40 CFR 63.2)
Are the boilers classified as industrial, commercial, or institutional boilers per §63.11237?

Do the boilers burn gaseous fuels as their normal fuel, and do they burn liquid fuel only during gas curtailment/supply interruption/startup/periodic testing/training with combined liquid-fuel use ≤ 48 hours per calendar year (i.e., do they meet the 'gas-fired boiler' definition)? (see 40 CFR 63.11237 and 63.11195(e))
Is any oil combustion beyond curtailment/testing (hours per year of liquid fuel use; frequency and purpose)? (compare actual oil use vs. the 48-hour limit in the gas-fired boiler definition)
Are the boilers electric utility steam generating units (EGUs) as defined in §63.11237 (e.g., >25 MW and producing electricity for sale and meeting the EGU criteria)?
Are the boilers specifically listed as affected sources in any other part 63 subpart or in a section 129 standard, or covered by subpart EEE or a 3005 SWDA permit? (see 40 CFR 63.11195(a)-(c))
Are the boilers subject to any federally enforceable limit that makes them 'limited-use boilers' (annual capacity factor ≤ 10%)? (if yes, obtain the enforceable permit language)

If subject to Subpart JJJJJJ, which compliance paths apply (performance testing, fuel analysis for mercury, work-practice/tune-up, monitoring) and what are the applicable initial compliance dates (e.g., construction dates relative to June 4, 2010) and testing/notification deadlines?

judge_text: {"score":1, "reason":"The answer includes the JJJJJJ gas-fired boiler exclusion and the 48‑hour/curtailment oil‑use condition (citing 63.11195(e) and 63.11237) and asks about hours of oil use, but it does not explicitly require that those oil‑use/curtailment conditions be made federally enforceable/‘locked in’ by permit as the EPA notes state."}

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If the stationary source is a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy of combined HAPs) then the definition of "major source" in this part applies for determining applicability of relevant subparts.
If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the owner/operator must perform the required performance tests within 180 days of the compliance date unless a waiver or extension applies.
If a relevant standard requires a continuous monitoring system (CMS), then the CMS is subject to the monitoring requirements and quality assurance/operation rules in this section.

candidates.title: Plywood and Composite Wood Products (PCWP) NESHAP (Subpart DDDD)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plywood and/or composite wood products (PCWP) manufacturing facility located at a major source of HAP, then this subpart applies to your affected source.

If combustion unit exhaust streams are routinely used to direct-fire PCWP dryers or lumber kilns, then those combustion units/exhaust streams are included in the affected source covered by this subpart.

If a process unit has a bypass stack that allows exhaust to temporarily vent to atmosphere while bypassing a control device used to meet add-on control compliance options, then process unit bypass stack monitoring and operating requirements apply.

If you operate direct-fired PCWP dryers (including direct wood-fired dryers), then annual combustion unit tune-ups and bypass stack monitoring for those combustion units are required as specified in the work practice requirements.

If you are subject to this subpart, then you must comply with subpart A provisions except as noted in Table 10 to this subpart and must meet the compliance options, operating requirements, and work practices when the process units are operating (with limited exceptions for specific startup/shutdown events).

candidates.title: Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional Boilers and Process Heaters (Subpart DDDDD)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an industrial, commercial, or institutional boiler or process heater located at or part of a major source of HAP (as defined in this part), then you are subject to this subpart unless excluded under § 63.7491.
If a boiler or process heater is one of the types listed in § 63.7491(a)–(n), then it is not subject to this subpart.

If the boiler or process heater is part of an affected source subject to another subpart (including units used as control devices to comply with other subparts), then it is not subject to this subpart.

If the boiler or process heater is used as a control device to comply with another subpart or part 60, part 61, or part 65 and at least 50 percent of its average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years is provided by regulated gas streams subject to another standard, then it is not subject to this subpart.

candidates.title: Boilers (Subpart JJJJJJ)

criteria.criterion: If a boiler is specifically listed as, or included in the definition of, an affected source in another standard under part 63, then that boiler is not subject to subpart JJJJJJ.

If a boiler is specifically listed as an affected source in a standard established under section 129 of the Clean Air Act or is a hazardous-waste boiler covered by subpart EEE, then it is not subject to this subpart.
If the boiler is gas-fired as defined in this subpart, then it is not subject to subpart JJJJJJ.

If a boiler is used as a control device to comply with another subpart or parts 60, 61, or 65 and at least 50 percent of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years is provided by regulated gas streams subject to another standard, then it is not subject to this subpart.
If the boiler is an electric or residential boiler or an EGU as defined in this subpart, then it is not subject to subpart JJJJJJ.

checklist: Is the facility a plywood and/or composite wood products (PCWP) manufacturing facility that bonds wood/fibers/resin to make panels or related products?
Is the facility located at a major source of HAP (potential to emit ≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined)?

Are the rotary gasifiers and secondary combustion chamber exhaust streams routinely used to direct-fire any PCWP dryers or lumber kilns (i.e., does most hot gas flow through the dryers during normal operation)?

Is any portion of the gasifier/combustion exhaust routinely diverted (bypassed) to a separate stack or used to heat thermal oil that vents to atmosphere (i.e., is there a process unit bypass stack or combustion unit bypass stack)?
Are the dryers explicitly included in the affected source under Subpart DDDD at this facility (do dryer vents/combustion units fall within the PCWP affected source boundary per § 63.2232)?

Are the gasifiers/combustion units physically part of or dedicated to the PCWP affected source (same contiguous area and common control) or are they separate units listed under another subpart or category?
Is any boiler/process heater at the facility specifically listed as an affected source in another part 63 subpart or under section 129 standards (which would exclude it from DDDDD/JJJJJJ)?
Do any of the combustion units burn hazardous waste (Subpart EEE) or qualify as recovery boilers, EGUs, residential, electric-only, or other Excluded types listed in § 63.7491 or § 63.11195?

For any boiler/process heater claimed as excluded because it is used as a control device to comply with another standard, was at least 50% of the average annual heat input during any 3 consecutive calendar years provided by regulated gas streams subject to another standard?
What fuels are burned in each combustion unit (wood residue, natural gas, oil, hazardous waste, electric) and do any units qualify as 'gas-fired' under subpart JJJJJJ?

Are there continuous monitoring systems (CEMS/COMS/CPMS) or bypass-stack monitors currently installed or required for the dryers/combustion units, and if so, are they installed and operated per the monitoring requirements?
For direct-fired dryers, are annual combustion unit tune-ups and the required monitoring of bypass usage being performed and documented as specified in the PCWP rule?

If claiming applicability/exemption based on construction/reconstruction dates or 'affected source' definitions, what are the relevant construction/startup dates for the dryers, gasifiers, and other process units?

candidates.title: Plywood and Composite Wood Products NESHAP

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a plywood and/or composite wood products (PCWP) manufacturing facility (which for purposes of this subpart includes facilities that manufacture dry veneer and lumber kilns located at any facility) and the PCWP manufacturing facility is located at a major source of HAP, then this subpart applies to you.

If you have an affected source (the collection of dryers, refiners, blenders, formers, presses, board coolers, and other process units associated with PCWP manufacturing, and which explicitly includes lumber kilns) at a PCWP manufacturing facility, then this subpart applies to each new, reconstructed, or existing affected source.

If an area source increases its emissions or its potential to emit such that it becomes a major source of HAP, then the facility must be in compliance with this subpart by October 1, 2007 or upon initial startup of the affected source as a major source, whichever is later.

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator of a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit any hazardous air pollutant and is subject to any standard, limitation, prohibition, or other federally enforceable requirement established pursuant to this part, then the provisions of this part apply to that owner or operator.

If a stationary source (or group of stationary sources within a contiguous area and under common control) emits or has the potential to emit, considering controls, 10 tons per year or more of any single HAP or 25 tons per year or more of any combination of HAP, then it meets the definition of a 'major source' for purposes of part 63.

If an area source that otherwise would be subject to a part 63 standard subsequently increases emissions (or potential to emit) such that it becomes a major source, then that source shall be subject to the notification requirements of this subpart and, upon becoming a major source again, is subject to the applicable major source requirements established under this part immediately upon becoming a major source again (provided the compliance date for the major source requirements has passed).

checklist: Calculate current and projected annual methanol emissions (tons/year) from the kilns: both actual emissions and potential to emit (PTE) considering physical and operational design and any federally enforceable limits in permits.
Calculate combined annual emissions (or PTE) of all HAPs to determine if facility meets major source thresholds (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy total).

Confirm whether your facility is a PCWP manufacturing facility as defined (does the facility manufacture plywood and/or composite wood products, or otherwise include dry veneer or lumber kilns that fall within the PCWP definitions?).
Confirm whether the lumber kilns at your site are included within the 'affected source' collection (dryers, refiners, blenders, formers, presses, board coolers, etc.) per the subpart's definition.

Determine whether the facility is currently classified as an area source or major source in your title V/State permit and whether any permit revision reclassifying the source to 'major' has been issued and the effective date of that reclassification.

Review your title V or other federally enforceable permit conditions to identify any enforceable emission limits or restrictions that legally cap potential to emit (these affect the major/area source determination).

If currently an area source that will exceed major thresholds, document the date emissions/PTE crossed the threshold and whether the facility has (or will have) 'initial startup as a major source' events—identify the compliance date you must meet per 40 CFR 63.2233(c).

Identify which process units (specific kilns) would constitute the affected source so you can determine which units would become subject and whether they are new, reconstructed, or existing (affects applicable compliance dates).

candidates.title: Chemical Manufacturing Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chemical manufacturing process unit (CMPU) located at an area source and Table 1 hazardous air pollutants are present in the CMPU at the concentrations specified in § 63.11494(a)(2) then the CMPU is subject to this subpart.

If an area source installed a federally-enforceable control device on an affected CMPU and that control device is necessary to maintain the source's emissions at area source levels then the source is required to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or 40 CFR part 71 as specified in this subpart.
If the operations are among those listed in paragraph (c)(1) through (c)(6) of § 63.11494 then those specified operations are not subject to this subpart.

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit any hazardous air pollutant and is subject to a standard established under part 63 then the provisions of this part apply to the owner or operator.

If an area-source standard promulgated under this part specifies whether area sources affected by that standard are excluded from, deferred from, or subject to title V permitting then that specification controls, and if a standard fails to specify permitting requirements then area sources subject to the standard will be subject to the requirement to obtain a title V permit.

If a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit, considering controls, 10 tons per year or more of any HAP or 25 tons per year or more of any combination of HAPs then it is a major source (and not an area source) for purposes of this part.

candidates.title: Chemical Preparations Area Sources

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a chemical preparations facility that is a stationary area source and the facility has at least one chemical preparations operation in target HAP service then this subpart applies to those chemical preparations operations located at the facility.

If you are an area source subject to this subpart then you are exempt from the obligation to obtain a permit under 40 CFR part 70 or part 71 provided you are not otherwise required by law to obtain such a permit, but you must continue to comply with the provisions of this subpart.
If the chemical preparations operations at your facility are subject to subpart VVVVVV or subpart CCCCCCC then you are exempt from the requirements specified in this subpart.

checklist: Confirm whether your facility is an area source or a major source using the definition in 40 CFR 63.2 (calculate actual and potential to emit of HAPs, including fugitive emissions, and include whether any physical or operational limits are federally enforceable).

Verify whether the affected equipment constitutes a CMPU as defined in § 63.11494(b) and whether Table 1 HAP are present at concentrations above the thresholds in § 63.11494(a)(2) (use SDS, supplier formulation data, or engineering assessment and use upper bound of concentration ranges).

Document whether any federally-enforceable control device has been installed on an affected CMPU (identify permitting or consent-order language, permit conditions, or other enforceable limitations establishing the control as federally enforceable).

Determine whether the federally-enforceable control device is necessary to maintain the source's emissions below major source thresholds (calculate potential to emit both with and without the control device in place and consider whether limits that make controls 'necessary' are legally enforceable).
Check whether your facility is otherwise required to obtain a title V permit under 40 CFR 70.3(a) or 71.3(a) independent of subpart VVVVVV (for example, State rules or other federal requirements).

If your operations could also fall under the chemical preparations subpart (BBBBBBB) or other area-source subparts, verify whether those subparts apply or provide a title V exemption (e.g., § 63.11579(f) exempts chemical preparations operations subject to VVVVVV).

If a federally-enforceable control device triggers title V under § 63.11494(e), determine the date your source became subject to that requirement and check the applicable title V application deadline in § 63.11494(e) (e.g., deadlines tied to dates specified in that paragraph).

Confirm whether any exemptions listed in § 63.11494(c)(1)–(6) apply to specific operations at your facility (research & development, QA/QC labs, ancillary activities, listed area-source categories, specified NAICS exclusions, etc.).

Retain records and calculations (material balances, engineering assessments, emissions estimates, permit language, SDS, dates of control installation) to demonstrate whether controls are federally enforceable and necessary to maintain area-source status.

candidates.title: Lead Acid Battery Manufacturing Plant Area Source Standards

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a lead acid battery manufacturing plant or a lead acid battery component manufacturing plant that is an area source of HAP emissions, then this subpart applies to your affected source.

If you are an existing affected source and a prior performance test was conducted using the same methods and either no process changes have been made since the test or you can demonstrate that the prior test results (with or without adjustments) reliably demonstrate compliance, then you are not required to conduct an initial performance test for that affected source.

If you elect to group similar affected sources that are of the same process type and have the same type of air pollution control device, then you may conduct subsequent performance tests on one representative affected source for that group in lieu of testing every unit (provided you prepare and submit the required testing plan for Administrator review and approval prior to testing).

If an initial performance test has been conducted, then you must conduct subsequent performance tests every 5 years (and, for sources that have not had a test within the last 5 years, within three years of February 23, 2023, subject to the exceptions in this section).

candidates.title: General Provisions (performance testing and waivers)

criteria.criterion: If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the owner or operator must perform required performance tests within 180 days of the compliance date unless a waiver of performance testing is obtained under this section or other specified exceptions apply.

If the owner or operator submits a written application for a waiver and the Administrator, in the Administrator's judgment, determines the source is meeting the relevant standard(s) on a continuous basis (or the source is subject to an extension of compliance or an extension request is pending), then an individual performance test may be waived.

If you request a waiver of an initial or subsequent performance test, then the waiver application must be submitted at least 60 days before the performance test if the site-specific test plan is not submitted and must include information justifying the waiver (e.g., technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality).
If the Administrator approves a waiver, then the Administrator may later cancel the waiver after notice, and approval does not abrogate the Administrator's authority under the Act.

checklist: Confirm the plant is a lead acid battery manufacturing plant or lead acid battery component manufacturing plant and is an area source of HAPs (to establish applicability to Subpart PPPPPP).
For each new Humidity Curing and Drying Oven Chamber: record the date construction/initial startup to determine new vs existing affected source status under §63.11422.
Identify whether each new oven is part of the same affected source (plant) that includes previously tested ovens (i.e., all equipment under common control in a contiguous area).

Locate and assemble prior performance test reports for the existing ovens: date of test, test methods used, test results, and test report (to show a prior performance test exists and which methods were used).

Determine whether any process changes have occurred since the prior performance tests for the same/similar ovens (changes to oven design, operating temperatures, feed materials, capture/ventilation, control devices, or other process parameters).

If relying on a prior test to avoid testing new ovens, document and be prepared to demonstrate how the prior test results (with or without adjustments) reliably represent compliance for the new ovens (e.g., similarity of process type, control device, operating conditions).

If you intend to group similar affected sources and test a representative unit, prepare a representative-testing plan that lists all grouped emission units, the process type and control device for each, the chosen representative unit, and dates of last tests, and submit it to the Administrator or delegated authority (note: §63.11423(c)(5)(iii) requires submission no later than 90 days prior to the first scheduled performance test).

If seeking a waiver of performance testing under §63.7(h), prepare a written waiver application that justifies the waiver (continuous compliance evidence or other justification) and submit it at least 60 days before the scheduled performance test if the site-specific test plan is not submitted.

Compile continuous compliance evidence to support a waiver request: monitoring records, inspection and maintenance records for control devices, opacity/visible emissions logs, baghouse/filter pressure-drop records, bag leak detector logs, and any prior performance test data.

Ensure you have records demonstrating operation and maintenance consistent with good air pollution control practices (operation/maintenance procedures, logs, corrective actions) as referenced in §63.11423(a)(4).

Verify control device types and configurations for the new ovens match those of previously tested units (same type of air pollution control device is required to group units under §63.11423(c)(5)(i)).

Confirm applicable submission and timing requirements: waiver application timing (≥60 days before test if no site-specific plan), representative test plan timing (≤90 days prior to scheduled representative test), and performance-test reporting deadlines (results reported in Notification of Compliance Status per applicable section).

Retain prior performance test records, monitoring data, and supporting documentation for at least 5 years to support waiver or grouping requests and to meet recordkeeping expectations for performance tests and waivers.

These elements capture the key reasons in the EPA notes."}

candidates.title: Stationary Combustion Turbines (Subpart YYYY)

criteria.criterion: If your stationary combustion turbine is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst, then you must petition the Administrator for operating limitations that you will monitor to demonstrate compliance with the formaldehyde emission limitation in Table 1 (or petition for approval of no additional operating limitations).

If you petition the Administrator for approval of additional operating limitations, then your petition must identify the specific parameters proposed, discuss how those parameters relate to HAP emissions and how limiting them will limit HAPs, explain how upper and/or lower values for the parameters will be established, describe the measurement and continuous monitoring methods and instrument accuracy/precision, and describe recalibration frequency and methods.

If you petition the Administrator for approval of no additional operating limitations, then your petition must identify parameters that could change, discuss any relationship to HAP emissions, explain why limitations cannot be established, describe available measurement/monitoring methods and recalibration, and explain why adopting parameters as operating limitations is infeasible, unreasonable, or unnecessary.

If your stationary combustion turbine is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst and you have an approved petition specifying parameters, then you must measure those operating parameters during the initial performance test and continuously monitor them thereafter to demonstrate compliance with the formaldehyde operating limitation.

If a performance test is required to demonstrate compliance, then performance tests must be conducted at high load defined as 100 percent ±10 percent, consist of three separate test runs each lasting at least 1 hour, and you must record process information necessary to document operating conditions during the test.

If you are required to conduct parametric monitoring to show continuous compliance, then you must conduct all parametric monitoring at all times the stationary combustion turbine is operating (except for monitor malfunctions, repairs, and required QA/QC activities) and you must not use data recorded during monitor malfunctions, associated repairs, and required QA/QC activities for meeting the subpart requirements.

If you are required to demonstrate continuous compliance with the emission and operating limitations, then you must do so according to the methods specified in Table 5 of this subpart and report each deviation as required.

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If you wish to use an alternative monitoring procedure (for example, using %Load and inlet air temperature instead of the monitoring specified in the subpart), then you must apply to the Administrator for approval and include a description addressing the monitoring elements in §63.2 and a performance evaluation test plan as required by §63.8(f).

If you intend to use an alternative test method or alternative monitoring method for a performance test or CMS performance evaluation, then you must notify the Administrator at least 60 days before the test, validate the alternative per Method 301 where applicable, and obtain Administrator approval (or await the statutory review periods specified in §63.7 and §63.8).

If you are required to use a continuous monitoring system (CMS), then you must develop and implement a CMS quality control program (written procedures), keep those procedures on record for the life of the affected source, and follow the CMS operation and maintenance and performance evaluation requirements in §63.8.

If monitoring data will be used for compliance determinations, then monitoring must be conducted as set forth in this section and the relevant standard and any alternative monitoring must be approved by the Administrator under §63.8(f).

checklist: Confirm the turbine is a lean premix gas-fired stationary combustion turbine covered by Subpart YYYY (verify configuration and fuel type).
Confirm the turbine construction/reconstruction date relative to regulatory cutoff (you stated constructed after January 14, 2003).
Confirm the turbine is not equipped with an oxidation catalyst (verify presence/absence of catalyst and any control devices).
Confirm whether the formaldehyde emission limitation in Table 1 of Subpart YYYY applies to this unit (new/reconstructed lean premix gas-fired turbines are subject per §63.6100).

Decide whether to petition for specific operating parameters (e.g., %Load and inlet air temperature T1) or to petition for approval of no additional operating limitations, and prepare the chosen petition before conducting the initial performance test (per §63.6120(e)).

If petitioning for parameters, prepare documentation addressing: identification of parameters; technical relationship between each parameter and HAP (formaldehyde) emissions; proposed upper/lower limit values and rationale; measurement and continuous monitoring methods and instrument accuracy/precision; and recalibration frequency and procedures (per §63.6120(f)(1)-(5)).

If petitioning for no additional limits, prepare documentation addressing parameters that could change, their relation to HAP emissions, why limits cannot be established, measurement/monitoring feasibility and recalibration, and why limits would be infeasible/unnecessary (per §63.6120(g)(1)-(7)).

Verify ability to measure %Load and inlet air temperature (T1) during the initial performance test and continuously thereafter (instrumentation, data logging, accuracy, precision, calibration records).
Ensure the initial performance test will not be conducted until after petition approval or disapproval by the Administrator (per §63.6120(e)).

Plan the initial performance test to meet performance test requirements (high load 100% ±10%, three runs each ≥1 hour, record necessary process information to document operating conditions) per §63.6120(c)-(d) and §63.7.

Prepare to continuously monitor the approved parameter(s) at all times the turbine is operating (except for permitted QA/QC or malfunctions) and to exclude data from malfunctions/repairs/QA activities when demonstrating compliance (per §63.6135(a)-(b)).

If an alternative monitoring procedure or alternative test method will be used (i.e., using %Load and T1 as surrogate operating limits), prepare and submit the application/plan required by §63.8(f)(4) including the performance evaluation test plan and allow required review periods (and Method 301 validation if applicable per §63.7(f)).

Assess whether a CMS quality control program is required (post-September 8, 2020 or if CMS is required) and prepare written procedures for CMS QA/QC, calibration, preventive maintenance, data recording/reporting, accuracy audits, and corrective action per §63.6125(e) and §63.8(d).

Ensure procedures for daily/periodic calibration checks and recordkeeping are in place for any sensors (load and temperature) and that calibration/recalibration frequency and methods meet descriptions in the petition and subpart requirements.

Prepare reporting and recordkeeping workflows to include semiannual compliance reports, Notification of Compliance Status with performance test results within 60 days of test completion, and records to support any deviations per §§63.6145 and 63.6150.
