candidates.title: Printing, Coating, Slashing, Dyeing, and Finishing of Fabric and Other Textiles (Subpart OOOO)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source that performs dyeing or finishing of fabric or other textiles and the affected source is a major source (or located at a major source), then Subpart OOOO applies to the dyeing/finishing affected source and to the finishing materials used there.

If the solvent is used as a thinning material for a coating or printing material (i.e., an organic solvent added after the material is received), then that solvent is a regulated 'thinning material' and must be included when determining compliance (and, for the compliant-material option for web coating/printing, such thinning and cleaning materials must contain no organic HAP).

If the solvent is purchased as part of the finishing material (i.e., is included in the finishing material as purchased or is an auxiliary added to the finish that is part of the purchased finishing material), then the solvent's organic HAP mass fraction counts toward the finishing material's mass fraction of organic HAP and must meet the applicable emission limit in Table 1 (or be included in emission-rate/add-on-control calculations) for dyeing/finishing operations.

If you choose the compliant-material option to demonstrate compliance, then you must evaluate regulated materials in the condition they are received from the supplier prior to any on-site alteration (so on-site dilution after receipt is not counted for the as-purchased demonstration), and you may rely on supplier/manufacturer formulation data for organic HAP content.

If you determine compliance by an emission-rate or add-on-controls option, then you must include all regulated materials (as defined in § 63.4371) used in the affected source when calculating the organic HAP emission rate and follow the emission-rate and control-credit procedures in §§ 63.4331–63.4341.

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If your facility is subject to a relevant standard under part 63 (for example Subpart OOOO), then Subpart A's general provisions (definitions, performance testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements) are part of the relevant standard and apply.

checklist: Identify which textile operations are performed at each affected source: web coating/printing, slashing, dyeing, and/or finishing (per 40 CFR 63.4281 and 63.4282).
Determine whether the affected source is a major source (PTE ≥ 10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥ 25 tpy combined HAP) per 40 CFR 63.2.

For each solvent used to dilute or formulate finishes, determine how it is used on-site: (a) purchased as part of the finishing material, (b) added on-site as a thinner to a coating/printing material, or (c) used solely as an equipment/surface cleaning solvent.

Obtain supplier/manufacturer formulation data (or perform Method 311/Method 24 testing) showing organic HAP mass fraction and mass fraction of solids for the finishing material and for the solvent as purchased (see 40 CFR 63.4321(e)).

If you add solvent on-site (dilution), document whether you intend to demonstrate compliance using the 'as-purchased' (compliant-material) basis or an emission-rate/add-on-control basis, since compliant-material demonstrations use materials in the condition received (40 CFR 63.4321(e)).
If using the compliant-material option for web coating/printing, verify that all thinning and cleaning materials as purchased contain no organic HAP (40 CFR 63.4321(a)(1)).

If using an emission-rate or add-on-controls option, compile monthly/rolling 12-month usage data (mass of each coating/printing/dyeing/finishing and solvent used), and be prepared to include any waste or wastewater credits, capture efficiencies, and control device DREs per §§ 63.4331–63.4341.

If taking credit for wastewater diversion or POTW discharge, document wastewater sampling, average organic HAP concentrations, and mass flow rates and confirm treatment/discharge destination per 40 CFR 63.4331(c).

If using solvent recovery/add-on controls, document solvent recovery system monitoring (mass recovered device), recovery efficiency calculations, and capture system performance as required in 40 CFR 63.4341(e)/(f).

Maintain records of material purchase specifications, on-site dilution practices (dates, volumes, batches), and the basis for organic HAP determinations (supplier data or test results) to support whichever compliance option you select.

This matches the EPA note that solvents used to dilute finishing materials are subject to the organic HAP emission limit."}

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Wood Building Products

criteria.criterion: if the facility applies surface coatings (including adhesives) to products that contain more than 50 percent by weight wood or wood fiber (excluding the weight of any glass components) and are used in the construction of residential, commercial, or institutional buildings (for example, doors, windows, and window components), then subject to Subpart QQQQ

if the affected source uses 4,170 liters (1,100 gallons) per year or more of coatings in the wood building products source category and the source is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source of HAP, then subject to Subpart QQQQ

if the surface coating operation meets any of the exclusion criteria listed in paragraphs (c)(1) through (c)(5) of §63.4681 (e.g., coating that is part of plywood/composite wood manufacturing subject to subpart DDDD; surface coating of wood furniture subject to subpart JJ; prefabricated home coating; noncommercial or research/laboratory coating; wood treatment using a retort), then not subject to Subpart QQQQ

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Miscellaneous Metal Parts and Products

criteria.criterion: if the operation performs surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts or products (metal components such as extruded aluminum structural components and similar metal parts), then subject to Subpart MMMM

if the affected source uses 946 liters (250 gallons) per year or more of coatings that contain HAP in the surface coating of miscellaneous metal parts and products and the source is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source of HAP, then subject to Subpart MMMM

if the coating operation meets any exclusion in paragraph (c)(1) through (c)(17) of §63.3881 (for example, the facility uses only coatings/thinners/cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP; coatings used in very small volumes; metal components that are subject to another surface-coating NESHAP listed in paragraph (c)), then not subject to Subpart MMMM
if the metal parts being coated are metal components of wood building products that meet the applicability criteria for Subpart QQQQ, then not subject to Subpart MMMM for those metal components

if the coatings applied to the metal parts meet the definition of high performance architectural coating or high temperature coating in §63.3981, then the operation falls within the high performance coating subcategory of Subpart MMMM (and Subpart MMMM still applies if other applicability criteria are met)

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: if a stationary source emits or has the potential to emit 10 tons per year or more of any single HAP or 25 tons per year or more of any combination of HAP, then it meets the definition of a major source in this part (relevant to determining applicability of subparts that apply only to major sources)
if a relevant subpart requires performance testing, then the performance testing requirements of §63.7 apply (including timing, notification, site-specific test plans, QA, and reporting)

if a relevant subpart requires continuous parameter or continuous monitoring systems, then the monitoring requirements of §63.8 apply (installation, operation, QA/QC, data reduction, and reporting requirements)

checklist: For wooden window components: confirm percent wood/wood-fiber by weight (exclude glass weight) for the coated items to verify >50% wood content
For wooden window components: confirm intended end use (are the components used in construction of residential, commercial, or institutional buildings?)

For wooden window components: total annual volume (liters or gallons) of all coatings used at the affected source (include adhesives, sealants, primers, topcoats, cleaning materials) to compare to the 4,170 L/yr threshold

For wooden window components: determine whether the coating operations are part of any excluded category listed at §63.4681(c) (e.g., part of plywood/composite wood manufacturing subject to subpart DDDD; wood furniture/cabinet manufacturing subject to subpart JJ; prefabricated homes; research/lab; retort wood treatment)
For aluminum window components: confirm that the coated items are metal parts (aluminum) and not excluded as metal components of wood building products that meet Subpart QQQQ applicability
For aluminum window components: determine whether the coatings used are 'high performance architectural coatings' (e.g., meet AAMA 605.2-2000) or otherwise meet the definitions in §63.3981

For aluminum window components: determine annual volume (liters or gallons) of coatings that contain organic HAP used on miscellaneous metal parts (count only HAP-containing coatings toward the 946 L/yr threshold per §63.3881(b)); separately track volumes of non-HAP coatings
Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP (calculate actual or potential to emit in tpy of individual and combined HAP to compare to 10 tpy / 25 tpy thresholds in §63.2)

Determine whether any coatings, thinners, or cleaning materials used contain organic HAP (if the facility uses only materials that contain no organic HAP as determined per §63.3941/definitions, Subpart MMMM may not apply under §63.3881(c)(1))

If using adhesives, determine whether they are reactive adhesives and whether the organic HAP mass fraction should be calculated as emitted (see definitions and special rules in §63.3981 and §63.4741(a)(4))

If the facility performs multiple surface-coating activities subject to different surface-coating NESHAPs, quantify coating activity by liters (or liters of solids) used to determine whether one subpart accounts for ≥90% (predominant activity) or ≥95% (for QQQQ alternative compliance) of coating usage as described in §§63.3881(e) and 63.4681(d)

Collect supplier/manufacturer formulation data and/or test data (Method 311, Method 24, ASTM methods) needed to determine mass fraction of organic HAP, volume fraction of coating solids, and density for coatings to apply the compliant-material or emission-rate calculations in §§63.4741 and 63.4742 (for QQQQ) and the definitions in §63.3981 (for MMMM)

Document whether any surface-coating operations are part of operations covered by other NESHAPs listed in exclusion paragraphs (e.g., subpart JJ, NNNN, RRRR, II, JJJJ, SSSS, VVVV, IIII) and collect supporting records to substantiate exclusion or to choose the appropriate NESHAP for compliance

If subject to an applicable subpart, confirm applicable performance testing and monitoring deadlines and prepare to meet §63.7 notification/site-specific test-plan and §63.8 monitoring/CPMS/CMS requirements

candidates.title: Aerospace Manufacturing and Rework Operations

criteria.criterion: If a facility is engaged, in whole or in part, in the manufacture or rework of commercial, civil, or military aerospace vehicles or components and is a major source as defined in § 63.2, then Subpart GG applies to the facility.
If an activity at the facility is a cleaning operation (hand-wipe, spray gun, or flush cleaning), then that activity is an affected source under this subpart.
If the cleaning is of electronic parts and assemblies, then the cleaning operation is exempt from the cleaning requirements of this subpart (i.e., not subject to § 63.744 requirements).

If the cleaning is of aircraft or ground support equipment fluid systems exposed to the fluid (including hydraulic fluid systems), then the cleaning operation is exempt from the cleaning requirements of this subpart.

If primers, topcoats, specialty coatings, chemical milling maskants, strippers, or cleaning solvents meet the definition of 'Non-HAP material', then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to those materials.

If a hand-wipe cleaning operation is not exempt, then the hand-wipe solvents must either meet the composition requirements in Table 1 of § 63.744(b)(1), have a composite vapor pressure ≤45 mm Hg at 20 °C as specified in § 63.744(b)(2), or be covered by an approved 60% usage reduction demonstration under § 63.744(b)(3).

If a spray-gun cleaning operation is not exempt, then the owner/operator must use one of the techniques specified in § 63.744(c)(1)–(c)(4) (enclosed system, nonatomized cleaning, disassembled-gun vat cleaning/soak, or atomizing capture device) and comply with the operational and inspection requirements.

If a flush cleaning operation is not exempt, then used cleaning solvent must be emptied each time into an enclosed container or collection system kept closed when not in use or into a system with equivalent emission control as required by § 63.744(d).

If an owner/operator uses an enclosed spray-gun cleaner under § 63.744(c)(1), then the enclosed spray-gun cleaner seals and other potential leak sources must be visually inspected at least once per month while in operation.

If a cleaning operation is subject to this subpart, then the owner/operator must keep the cleaning-solvent identity, vapor pressure, and documentation of organic HAP constituents and comply with the cleaning-specific recordkeeping elements in § 63.752(b) and the semiannual reporting in § 63.753(b).

If solvent composition or vapor pressure determinations are needed to demonstrate compliance with the hand-wipe solvent requirements, then composition is demonstrated by manufacturer's data per § 63.750(a) and composite vapor pressure for blends is determined per § 63.750(b).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If a source is subject to Subpart GG, then the owner/operator must also comply with the specified General Provisions (e.g., § 63.4, § 63.5, § 63.6) as listed in § 63.743(a) except where § 63.743(a) provides otherwise.
If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then the owner/operator must perform performance testing in accordance with § 63.7 within the applicable timeframes and procedural requirements.

If a continuous monitoring system (CMS) or other monitoring is required by a relevant standard, then monitoring must be conducted and the CMS operated, maintained, and evaluated according to § 63.8 and the monitoring provisions of the relevant standard.

checklist: Determine whether the facility is a major source under 40 CFR 63.2 (potential to emit ≥10 tpy of any single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAPs).

Confirm whether the facility performs manufacture or rework of aerospace vehicles or components (per Subpart GG definition of aerospace facility/aerospace vehicle or component) and identify which items are processed (note: electronic components are excluded from the aerospace vehicle/component definition).

List all cleaning activities (hand-wipe, spray-gun, flush) and the specific items cleaned (electronic assemblies, printed circuit boards, aircraft hydraulic systems, engine components, ground support equipment, etc.).

For each cleaning activity, identify whether it falls into any exemption in § 63.744(e) (e.g., cleaning electronic parts and assemblies; cleaning aircraft fluid/hydraulic systems; R&D, lab testing; confined spaces; energized electrical systems, Montreal Protocol essential uses).

Collect manufacturer data/MSDS for the azeotropic blend (hydrofluoroether + dichloroethylene): identify all components, determine whether any are organic HAPs, whether any are exempt solvents under 40 CFR 51.100, and whether the blend meets the 'Non-HAP material' definition per § 63.742.

If using the azeotropic blend for hand-wipe cleaning, calculate composite vapor pressure at 20 °C (per § 63.750(b)) and/or confirm composition vs. Table 1 (aqueous or hydrocarbon-based) to see which compliance path applies.

If any hand-wipe solvents do not meet the composition or vapor-pressure criteria, determine whether you will implement an approved 60% volume reduction baseline plan per § 63.744(b)(3) and secure State/Administrator approval if required.

If spray-gun cleaning is performed, document which cleaning technique is used (enclosed gun cleaner, nonatomized pressure-pot purge, disassembled vat soak, atomizing capture device) and, if using an enclosed cleaner, implement monthly visual seal/leak inspections and repair leaks within 15 days as required by § 63.751(a).
If flush cleaning is performed, verify that used solvent is emptied each time into an enclosed, closed container or an equivalent emission-control system per § 63.744(d).

Maintain records required by § 63.752(b) for cleaning operations: solvent identity, vapor pressure, HAP constituents, monthly volumes where applicable, and keep these records for the required retention period.

Plan to submit semiannual cleaning operation reports per § 63.753(b) (instances of noncompliant solvent use, new cleaning solvents, noncompliant spray-gun methods, leaking enclosed cleaners >15 days, or a statement of compliance).

If you will use control devices (e.g., carbon adsorbers or incinerators) to meet standards for non-exempt cleaning/coating/depaiting activities, identify required initial performance tests and ongoing monitoring/operating parameter setting obligations per § 63.751 and § 63.750(g)/(h).

If you intend to rely on coating/solvent manufacturer's data to demonstrate compliance, assemble and retain the manufacturer's supplied formulation data, EPA Method 24/311 test results as applicable (see § 63.750 references), and be prepared for Method 24 or Method 311 verification during inspections.

Check low-volume exemptions and other numeric exemptions that might apply to coatings/related materials (e.g., small annual volumes) and document annual purchase/use to confirm eligibility per § 63.741(g) and related provisions.

candidates.title: Subpart CC (Petroleum Refining miscellaneous process vents and flares)

criteria.criterion: if the emission points are at a petroleum refining process unit located at a plant site that is a major source and the equipment emits or contains one or more hazardous air pollutants listed in Table 1, then subpart CC applies to the affected source

if a vent stream meets the definition of a miscellaneous process vent and the total organic HAP concentration is greater than or equal to 20 ppmv and the total VOC/TOC emission rate at the outlet of the final recovery device meets the Group 1 thresholds (≥33 kg/day for existing sources or ≥6.8 kg/day for new sources), then the vent is a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent and must comply with the Group 1 requirements in this subpart

if the owner/operator elects to control a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent with a control device (other than a flare), then the owner/operator must reduce organic HAP emissions by 98 weight‑percent or to a concentration of 20 ppmv (dry, corrected to 3% O2), whichever is less stringent

if a boiler or process heater is used to comply with the 98% reduction or 20 ppmv limit, then the vent stream must be introduced into the flame zone (or in a location such that the required reduction or concentration is achieved)

if an owner/operator of a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent seeks to monitor parameters other than those specified in §63.644(a), then the owner/operator may request approval for alternative monitoring parameters as provided in §63.644(b)

candidates.title: Subpart G (Process vent provisions—chemical/process industry)

criteria.criterion: if a vent is a Group 1 process vent, then the owner/operator must either control with a flare (per the applicable flare rules) or reduce total organic HAP by 98 weight‑percent or to a concentration of 20 ppmv (dry, corrected to 3% O2) as provided in §63.113(a)(1)–(2)

if a combustion device, recovery device, or recapture device is used to comply with the Group 1 process vent standard, then the owner/operator must install, operate, calibrate, and maintain the monitoring equipment specified for that device in §63.114(a) or §63.114(b), unless approval to monitor other parameters is requested

if the owner/operator seeks to monitor parameters other than those listed in §63.114(a) or (b) for a process vent or recovery device, then the owner/operator must request approval of alternative monitoring under §63.114(c)

if a process vent meets the defined conditions to be designated a maintenance vent, then the owner/operator may designate it as a maintenance vent and comply only with the maintenance-vent provisions in §63.113(k) (rather than the Group 1/Group 2 requirements)

candidates.title: Subpart A (General Provisions — performance testing and alternative approaches)

criteria.criterion: if an owner/operator demonstrates that an alternative means of emission limitation will achieve emission reductions at least equivalent to the promulgated standard, then the Administrator may permit the use of that alternative emission standard after notice and opportunity for comment per §63.6(g)

if an owner/operator proposes to use alternative monitoring procedures or parameters, then the owner/operator must submit the required validation/requests and, where applicable, site‑specific test plans and performance tests in accordance with §63.7 and the alternative‑monitoring provisions of §63.8(f)

if the owner/operator is required to perform performance testing to demonstrate compliance (including for an alternative monitoring approach), then the performance testing must be conducted and reported according to the timing, QA, and plan submittal requirements in §63.7

checklist: Verify the plant is a CAA section 112 major source (plant‑site level).
Identify whether the orthoxylene rerun column vent is part of a petroleum refining process unit at that plant site.
Measure or compile the vent's total organic HAP concentration (ppmv) at the outlet of any final recovery device and determine whether it is ≥20 ppmv.

Calculate the vent's TOC/total organic HAP emission rate (kg/day or lb/hr) at the outlet of any final recovery device to determine Group 1 thresholds (≥33 kg/day existing, ≥6.8 kg/day new) or the mass‑flow thresholds in Subpart G.
Determine whether the vent is routed to the refinery fuel gas system (which may be excluded) or directly to a control device or atmosphere.

Determine which control device is used or proposed (flare, incinerator/catalytic incinerator, boiler/process heater, absorber/condenser/adsorber) and whether the vent stream will be introduced into the flame zone if a boiler/process heater is proposed.

Assemble performance test data (or plan) showing either ≥98 wt% reduction of organic HAP or an outlet concentration ≤20 ppmv (dry, corrected to 3% O2), and document the measurement method (organic HAP or TOC) to be used for compliance determinations.

If using a flare, verify readiness to meet Subpart CC flare requirements (pilot flame monitoring, visible emissions, NHV/Vtip/NHVcz/NHVdil monitoring and calculations) per §63.670 and recordkeeping/reporting needs.

If proposing alternative monitoring parameters (different from those in §63.644(a) or §63.114(a)/(b)), prepare and be ready to submit a request and justification (including site‑specific test/monitoring plan and QA procedures) as allowed by §63.644(b) or §63.114(c) and the Subpart A provisions on alternatives (§63.7 and §63.8(f)).
Confirm whether the vent is a maintenance vent situation (only used during startup/shutdown/maintenance/inspection) and whether maintenance‑vent conditions in the applicable subpart would apply.

Compile the Notification of Compliance Status / performance test and monitoring plan materials required for submission if pursuing an alternative monitoring plan or alternative emission limitation (including QA/QC, sampling schedule, and calculations).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If an affected source is subject to a relevant standard under part 63, then Subpart A performance testing provisions (including timing and notification) apply to that source's required performance tests.

If the relevant standard requires continuous monitoring systems (CEMS/CMS/COMS) or other continuous parameter monitoring, then the CMS operation, quality assurance, performance-evaluation, alternative-monitoring, and data-reduction requirements of § 63.8 apply.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Waste Combustors (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If you operate a hazardous waste incinerator (which for Subpart EEE includes all associated firing systems and air pollution control devices), then the emission standards, operating requirements, testing, and monitoring requirements in Subpart EEE apply to that combustor.

If you conduct a comprehensive performance test to demonstrate compliance, then you must use the test to establish operating parameter limits (including parameters necessary to ensure good operation of each hazardous waste firing system) based on the test run averages.

If you plan to feed any material to the combustor, then prior to feeding you must obtain and follow a feedstream analysis (including viscosity or a description of the physical form for each feedstream) and document how you will use those analyses to demonstrate compliance with feedrate and operating-parameter limits.

If you want to waive an operating parameter limit (or propose an alternative monitoring requirement) that is required by this subpart, then you may submit an application to the Administrator with the comprehensive performance test plan showing justification, proposed alternative or waiver, and documentation that the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance; the Administrator will review timing and content per § 63.1209(g)(1)(iii).

If your combustor is equipped with a wet scrubber for hydrogen chloride and chlorine control and the scrubber is a low-energy wet scrubber, then you must establish a minimum liquid feed pressure limit based on the manufacturer's specifications and comply with that limit on an hourly rolling average.

If you seek to waive monitoring of the wet-scrubber liquid feed pressure specifically, then you must follow the general waiver/alternative monitoring application procedures in § 63.1209(g)(1)(ii)–(iii) (submit with the comprehensive performance test plan, include data and justification demonstrating equivalence or that the parameter is not needed to ensure compliance).

checklist: Confirm whether the unit is a hazardous waste incinerator as defined in 40 CFR 63.1201 (i.e., incinerator includes all associated firing systems and air pollution control devices).
Document the firing system type (fluidized bed with simple lances) and whether hazardous waste is fed as pumpable liquid, slurry, or other physical form.

Obtain representative feedstream analyses for each waste/feedstream (as-fired) including measured viscosity at feed temperature or a clear description of physical form, chlorine content, and other relevant constituents per 40 CFR 63.1207(f)(1)(i) and 63.1209(c)(1).

Record normal and maximum ranges for waste fuel delivery pressure, atomization pressure, and any carrier-fluid or nozzle pressure during typical and upset operation (to support establishing limits or a waiver request).

Determine whether the firing system operating parameters (e.g., viscosity, delivery pressure, atomization pressure) were used to establish operating-parameter limits during any prior comprehensive performance test or must be established in the upcoming test per 40 CFR 63.1207/63.1209(j).

Identify whether the wet scrubber controlling HCl/Cl2 is a high-energy or low-energy wet scrubber and obtain the manufacturer's specified minimum liquid feed pressure and other recommended operating specs.
Document current scrubber monitoring: do you already monitor liquid feed pressure (with recorder) and pH and pressure drop as described in 40 CFR 63.1209(o)(3)?

Decide whether you will request a waiver or alternative monitoring: if so, prepare the application package to include data showing technical justification, alternative monitoring approach, and demonstration that the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance; schedule submission with the comprehensive performance test plan per 40 CFR 63.1209(g)(1)(iii).
Verify AWFCO interlocks and whether the parameter(s) you propose to waive are interlocked with AWFCO (if applicable) per automatic waste feed cutoff requirements in 40 CFR 63.1206(c)(3).

Prepare the comprehensive performance test plan to (a) include viscosity/physical-form data per 40 CFR 63.1207(f)(1)(i), (b) document proposed operating-parameter limits (or proposed waivers/alternatives), and (c) show how you will ensure the test conditions represent normal or higher-than-normal chlorine feedrates and other parameters as required by 40 CFR 63.1207(g)(1)(i).

Assemble monitoring/QA documentation demonstrating that any alternative monitoring will meet the CMS/CEMS quality assurance, performance-evaluation, and reporting expectations of 40 CFR part 63 Subpart A (§ 63.8) and the performance test procedures (§ 63.7).

If you will claim that an operating-parameter limit is unnecessary, compile data showing that omission of that limit would still ensure compliance with the applicable emission standard (e.g., emissions data, system removal efficiency calculations, variability analyses) to support the Administrator review.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Iron and Steel Foundries (NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If you have an existing affected source, then you must comply with each emissions limitation, work practice standard, and operation and maintenance requirement in this subpart no later than April 23, 2007.

If you are required to conduct a performance test to demonstrate initial compliance with the emissions limitations in §63.7690, then you must conduct that performance test no later than 180 calendar days after the compliance date specified in §63.7683.

If you conducted a performance test that you intend to use for initial compliance, then the test must have been conducted under conditions representative of normal operations (excluding startup, shutdown, and malfunction), with process information recorded to document and support that those conditions represent normal operation and made available to the Administrator upon request.

If you are determining compliance for PM from a pouring area or pouring station by performance testing, then you must follow the PM test methods and procedures in §63.7732(b), including collecting a minimum sample volume of 60 dscf per PM sampling run and obtaining a minimum of three valid test runs for the performance test.

If you seek to demonstrate initial compliance for a pouring station at an existing iron and steel foundry by PM concentration, then the average PM concentration determined according to §63.7732(b) must not have exceeded 0.010 gr/dscf.

If you intend to use a performance test (including one conducted before the compliance date) as your initial compliance demonstration, then you must submit the notification of compliance status including the performance test results before the close of business on the 60th calendar day following completion of the performance test (unless other subpart-specified timing applies).

candidates.title: General Provisions (Performance testing and monitoring requirements)

criteria.criterion: If a relevant standard requires performance testing, then, except as provided in this section, the owner or operator must perform the required performance tests within 180 days of the compliance date for the source.

If you schedule a performance test, then you must notify the Administrator in writing of your intention to conduct the performance test at least 60 calendar days before the performance test is initially scheduled to begin (unless an alternative timing/arrangement has been approved).

If you perform a required performance test, then the test must be conducted under conditions the Administrator specifies to represent normal operating performance and operations during startup, shutdown, and malfunction shall not constitute representative conditions for the test.

If you conduct a required performance test, then you must follow the quality assurance provisions (site-specific test plan on request, performance audit/audit-sample requirements, retention of test records) and report the test results to the Administrator within the timeframe required by the relevant standard (generally within 60 days after completion), and retain performance test records for at least 5 years.

checklist: Is the foundry an existing affected source (commencement of construction or reconstruction before December 23, 2002)?

What is the exact date of the April 2005 PM stack test (day/month/year) and the tested emission point (identify stack/duct and whether it's the outlet of a control device or the source outlet prior to atmospheric release)?
Was a notification of intent to conduct the performance test submitted to the Administrator at least 60 calendar days before the April 2005 test (per 40 CFR 63.7(b) / 63.7750(d))?

Were the specific test methods and procedures required by 40 CFR 63.7732(b) for PM followed (Methods 1/1A for port selection, Method 2-series for flow, Method 3-series for molecular weight, Method 4 for moisture, Method 5-series front-half for PM)?
Did each PM sampling run collect at least 60 dscf and did the test include a minimum of three valid test runs as required by 40 CFR 63.7732(b)(2)?

Were the test operating conditions representative of normal operations (no startup/shutdown/malfunction), and is there contemporaneous process documentation and an explanation supporting representativeness as required by 40 CFR 63.7732(a)?

Was the production rate (mass of metal charged or other relevant production metric used in calculations) measured and recorded for each test run, and were those rates representative of current routine production capability?

Were required QA elements followed (site-specific test plan if requested, performance audit/audit sample where applicable, chain-of-custody, raw data, and example calculations) per 40 CFR 63.7(c) and 63.7(g)?

Was the performance test report and notification of compliance status (including test results) submitted to the Administrator (or permitting authority) within the required period after test completion (generally within 60 days) as required by 40 CFR 63.7(g)(1) and 63.7750(e)(2)?
Are the performance test records and supporting information retained and available for inspection for at least 5 years as required by 40 CFR 63.7(g)(3)?

If the April 2005 test combined exhaust streams or used a control device, were the applicable combination or flow-weighting procedures and calculations in 40 CFR 63.7732(h) (or other relevant paragraphs) applied and documented?

If an alternative test method was used for any measurement, was the Administrator notified at least 60 days before the test and was Method 301 validation or Administrator approval completed per 40 CFR 63.7(f)?

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a relevant subpart requires use of a CEMS and does not specify a different averaging time, then CEMS data for pollutants other than opacity shall be reduced to 1-hour averages computed from four or more data points equally spaced over each 1-hour period.

If a continuous monitoring system (CEMS) other than a CPMS is required by a relevant standard, then the system must complete a minimum of one cycle of operation (sampling, analyzing, and data recording) for each successive 15-minute period.

candidates.title: Mercury Cell Chlor‑Alkali and Mercury Recovery Facilities (Subpart IIIII)

criteria.criterion: If you choose the continuous monitoring option for a mercury thermal recovery unit vent, then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration for each operating day as the arithmetic average of the 15-minute mercury concentration measurements (Equation 2).

If you choose the periodic monitoring option for a mercury thermal recovery unit vent, then you must demonstrate continuous compliance using the periodic procedures in §63.8234(b) (test-run concentration calculations and averaging per Equations 6 and 7).

If you are subject to the mercury thermal recovery unit vent limits in §63.8190(a)(3), then you must maintain the outlet mercury daily-average concentration at or below the applicable limit and obtain that concentration by monitoring under either the continuous or periodic monitoring options specified in §63.8244.

If you use the continuous monitoring option for by-product hydrogen streams, end box vents, or mercury thermal recovery unit vents, then you must collect mercury concentration data representing at least 75 percent of the 15-minute periods in each operating day (data during malfunctions/QA not counting toward the 75 percent requirement).

If you select the continuous mercury monitoring option, then each mercury continuous emissions monitor must sample, analyze, and record mercury concentration at least once every 15 minutes and meet the detector sensitivity requirements specified in §63.8242(a)(1)–(2).

candidates.title: Electric Utility Steam Generating Units and Hg CEMS Averaging (Subpart UUUUU)

criteria.criterion: If you are subject to Subpart UUUUU and you use a CEMS (or sorbent trap monitoring) to measure Hg emissions, then you must demonstrate continuous compliance by using all quality-assured hourly data to calculate the arithmetic average emissions rate on a continuous 30-boiler operating day rolling average basis (or 90-boiler operating day if alternate Hg averaging applies), updated at the end of each new boiler operating day.

candidates.title: Primary Copper Smelting (Subpart QQQ)

criteria.criterion: If you are subject to the mercury emissions provisions in this subpart and you use a Hg CEMS, then you must determine the average mercury concentration on a 6-hour rolling basis when using the Hg CEMS to demonstrate continuous compliance.

If you use a Hg CEMS under this subpart, then you must install and operate the Hg CEMS in accordance with Performance Specification 12A and follow the Procedure 5 QA/QC requirements and continuously measure and record exhaust gas flow rate as specified.

checklist: Is this emission point a mercury thermal recovery unit vent or part of a mercury cell chlor‑alkali production facility (potential applicability to Subpart IIIII), an EGU subject to Subpart UUUUU, or a copper smelting source subject to Subpart QQQ? (determine applicable subpart)
Which monitoring option have you chosen under the applicable subpart: continuous Hg CEMS (or mercury continuous emissions monitor) or periodic (stack test / sorbent trap) monitoring?

If continuous monitoring: does your Hg monitor provide at least one measurement every 15 minutes and meet the detector sensitivity requirements (0.1 µg/m3 or 0.5× performance-test level) required by §63.8242(a)?
If continuous monitoring under Subpart IIIII: can your monitor record valid data for at least 75% of the 15‑minute periods in each operating day (excluding malfunctions, QA/repair periods)?
If periodic monitoring under Subpart IIIII: which test method(s) will you use (Method 101/101A/102) and will you follow the sample/run averaging procedures in §63.8234(b) (Equations 6–7)?
Is your final control device a nonregenerable carbon adsorber (that changes certain periodic monitoring requirements in §63.8244(b))?

If subject to Subpart UUUUU and using CEMS or sorbent trap for Hg: does your system produce hourly, quality-assured data and are you prepared to calculate the required 30- (or 90-) operating‑day rolling average from hourly data?
If subject to Subpart QQQ and using Hg CEMS: are you prepared to apply a 6‑hour rolling average and meet PS12A and Procedure 5 QA/QC and continuous flow monitoring requirements?

Which emission limit applies to your unit (e.g., Subpart IIIII mercury recovery limits in §63.8190(a)(3): 23 mg/dscm oven-type or 4 mg/dscm non-oven-type) and what averaging time is specified by the applicable subpart?
Does your monitoring/data-reduction plan and recordkeeping account for exclusion of data during monitor malfunctions, QA/repair, and out-of-control periods per §63.8244(a) and §63.8(g)(5)?

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The submission includes the key EPA rationale: Subpart IIIII requires calculating a daily-average mercury concentration from 15‑minute values for mercury thermal recovery unit vents, and it also cites the Subpart A default 1‑hour CEMS averaging rule (and other subparts with different averaging times) that can cause the apparent hourly-average confusion. Thus the EPA Notes’ main points are captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate one or more miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) at a major source of HAP, then the requirements of this subpart FFFF apply to those MCPU.

If your process has batch process vents, then you must maintain the records specified in § 63.2525 (including records of each operating scenario, whether each batch was a standard batch, and estimated emissions for nonstandard batches) unless an exemption in § 63.2525(e)(1) applies.

If you wish to request EPA approval for items listed in § 63.2520(c)(1)–(8) (for example, setting operating limits for parameters other than those specified or providing data/rationale for engineering assessments), then you must submit a precompliance report under § 63.2520(c) and EPA will approve or disapprove it within 90 days.

If you documented in your Notification of Compliance Status that non-reactive organic HAP are the only HAP used in the process and usage is less than 10,000 lb/yr, then you may keep records of the amount used and calculate a daily rolling annual sum no less frequently than monthly instead of the full batch-by-batch records.

If you documented in your Notification of Compliance Status that total uncontrolled organic HAP emissions from the batch process vents will be less than 1,000 lb/yr for the anticipated number of standard batches, then you must keep records of the number of batches operated and calculate a daily rolling annual sum of batches operated no less frequently than monthly (and begin more detailed recordkeeping if that threshold is exceeded).

If none of the exceptions in § 63.2525(e)(1)–(3) apply, then you must keep per-batch records (day each batch completed and whether each batch was a standard batch, estimated uncontrolled and controlled emissions for nonstandard batches, and daily 365-day rolling summations of emissions or correlating records) as specified in § 63.2525(e)(4).

If you change any element of an operating scenario (except the list at § 63.2525(b)(5)), then that change constitutes a new operating scenario for reporting purposes and must be reported as required in § 63.2525(b)(8) and § 63.2520(e)(7).

If you intend to use emissions averaging or otherwise alter how batches are treated for debits/credits, then follow the emissions averaging provisions and batch emissions-per-standard-batch calculation rules in § 63.2500 (including the requirement to estimate uncontrolled emissions for a standard batch using the procedures in § 63.1257(d)(2)(i) and (ii) as modified by § 63.2500(e)).

candidates.title: General Provisions

criteria.criterion: If you want to use an alternative test method for a required performance test, then you must notify the Administrator at least 60 days before the test, validate the alternative using Method 301, and submit validation results as required by § 63.7(f).

If you want EPA approval of alternative monitoring procedures or minor/intermediate/major changes to monitoring, then you must submit an application that describes the proposed alternative and a performance evaluation test plan (if required) at least 60 days before the evaluation or as otherwise specified, and the Administrator will notify approval or intended disapproval as described in § 63.8(f).

If you wish to request approval to set operating limits for parameters other than those specified in §§ 63.2455 through 63.2485, then you may submit that request either in the Subpart FFFF precompliance report under § 63.2520(c)(1) or according to the alternative approval procedures in § 63.8(f).

If you want a waiver of a required performance test, then you must apply in writing and meet the timing and submittal requirements in § 63.7(h) (e.g., submit at least 60 days before the test date if a site-specific test plan is not submitted).

checklist: Determine whether your process(es) are MCPU as defined (§ 63.2550) and whether they are located at or part of a major source (§ 63.2435(a)).

Identify all batch process vents and calculate uncontrolled organic HAP emissions per batch and in the aggregate to determine Group 1 vs Group 2 status following § 63.2460(b) (use procedures in § 63.1257(d)(2)(i)/(ii) as directed by § 63.2460).
Decide whether non-reactive organic HAP are the only HAP and whether usage is <10,000 lb/yr (to evaluate applicability of § 63.2525(e)(2) alternative recordkeeping).
Estimate uncontrolled organic HAP emissions for the anticipated number of standard batches to check whether the <1,000 lb/yr threshold of § 63.2525(e)(3) applies.

Assemble current operating scenarios and the documented 'standard batch' definition(s) (process description; equipment; vents/routing; control devices; monitoring/parametric levels; calculations/engineering analyses) required by § 63.2525(b) and (c).

If you want EPA approval to alter operating-limit/monitoring/recordkeeping practices (e.g., define/use multiple standard batches), prepare a precompliance report per § 63.2520(c) containing the relevant data, calculations, and rationale (or prepare an alternative monitoring/test application per § 63.8(f) if pursuing that route).

Prepare the Notification of Compliance Status (NOCS) with all required items (including all operating scenarios) and note that NOCS is due no later than 150 days after the applicable compliance date (§ 63.2520(d)(1)–(2)).

If relying on simplified batch recordkeeping (counts or material usage) under § 63.2525(e)(2)–(3), ensure the monthly rolling annual calculations are implemented and documented so you can revert to simplified records only if thresholds remain below the limits for one year as specified.

If requesting alternative test methods or monitoring procedures, prepare Method 301 validation materials (for alternative test methods) or a site-specific performance evaluation test plan and be ready to submit at least 60 days before the planned test/evaluation (§ 63.7(f), § 63.8(f)).

Verify that any change to an operating-scenario element that is not within the standard-batch range will be treated as a new operating scenario and must be reported per § 63.2525(b)(8) and § 63.2520(e)(7).

Inventory what records you already keep vs. records explicitly required in § 63.2525 (e.g., per-batch standard/nonstandard designation, emissions estimates for nonstandard batches, daily 365-day rolling summaries) to identify exactly what you are requesting to modify.

OUR ANSWER does capture that the facility can request approvals/modify recordkeeping via the Subpart FFFF precompliance report (§63.2520(c)) and §63.8(f) alternative procedures (i.e., the general ability to request changes), but it does not cite or mention 40 CFR 63.10(f) specifically, so the exact EPA-cited authority is not reflected."}

candidates.title: Pharmaceutical manufacturing operations (Pharmaceuticals NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If the facility's manufacturing produces a 'pharmaceutical product' (including any material described by SIC code 2833 or 2834, or any material whose manufacturing process is described by NAICS 325411 or 325412, or an active ingredient/precursor as defined) then the facility is subject to Subpart GGG.

If the facility's operations constitute 'pharmaceutical manufacturing operations' (the facilitywide collection of PMPU and associated equipment used for manufacturing pharmaceutical products) then the facility is subject to Subpart GGG.
If the facility is a research and development facility whose primary purpose is R&D (as defined) then the facility may be excluded from applicability to pharmaceutical manufacturing rules.

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (MCPU / MON Rule)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU) that is located at, or is part of, a major source of HAP then you are subject to Subpart FFFF.

If the process unit produces materials described by the listed SIC (1987) codes (e.g., 282–289, 386) or by NAICS 325, and the MCPU processes, uses, or generates any of the organic HAP listed in section 112(b) or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP, and the MCPU is not an affected source under another subpart, then the unit meets the definition of an MCPU and Subpart FFFF applies.

If the operation qualifies for one of the explicit exemptions (for example, research and development facilities or the other operations listed in § 63.2435(c)) then the requirements of Subpart FFFF do not apply.

candidates.title: HCl production (HCl production NESHAP)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an HCl production facility that produces a liquid HCl product at a concentration of 30 weight percent or greater during normal operations and is located at, or part of, a major source of HAP, then Subpart NNNNN applies to that HCl production facility.
If an HCl production facility is also subject to NESHAP under one of the listed subparts (including Subpart GGG among others) then the HCl production facility is not subject to Subpart NNNNN.

candidates.title: General Provisions (definitions, performance testing, monitoring)

criteria.criterion: If a facility or affected source is subject to any subpart standard under this part, then the General Provisions in Subpart A (definitions of affected source/major source and performance testing and monitoring requirements) apply as specified in those provisions.

checklist: Is the material you produce (glucosamine hydrochloride) a 'pharmaceutical product' as defined (e.g., described by SIC 2833 or 2834, or produced by processes under NAICS 325411/325412) or is it used primarily as an active ingredient/precursor for pharmaceuticals?
What is the plant's primary SIC code and NAICS code for the operations producing glucosamine HCl (verify whether SIC 2833 or 2834 or NAICS 325411/325412 applies)?

Does your process constitute pharmaceutical manufacturing operations (facilitywide collection of PMPUs and associated equipment) or instead a miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process unit (MCPU)?
Do your processes produce, use, or generate any organic HAP (section 112(b)) or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP (e.g., HCl, Cl2) in the MCPU or process vents?
Is HCl produced on-site as a product (liquid HCl) at ≥30 wt% during normal operations, or is HCl only used/consumed as a reagent?
Is the HCl production (if any) routed, recycled, or otherwise excluded from being an HCl 'emission stream' per the HCl rule definitions (i.e., is it recycled prior to atmospheric discharge)?
Is the facility a major source of HAP (determine potential-to-emit and whether single HAP ≥10 tpy or combined HAP ≥25 tpy)?
Are any of the listed exemptions applicable (e.g., research & development status, specific NAICS exemptions listed for Subpart FFFF)?
Are any process units already regulated under another specific subpart that would preclude MCPU or HCl-subpart applicability (e.g., storage tanks or processes assigned to other subparts)?

For batch vs continuous: are emissions from batch process vents above the thresholds for Group 1/Group 2 designations (to determine specific FFFF obligations) — gather annual uncontrolled emissions estimates and operational mode (batch/continuous).
If considering Subpart NNNNN applicability, confirm whether HCl storage/transfer operations and transfer racks have predominant use tied to an HCl production unit.

Inventory and quantify HAP consumed, generated, and emitted (annual consumption and emissions) to support major-source determination and Group status under FFFF or to determine whether process vent concentrations/mass rates meet thresholds.

OUR ANSWER includes Subpart FFFF criteria that capture the key bases for that determination (MCPU at a major HAP source, applicability by SIC/NAICS and by processing/using/generating organic HAP or hydrogen halide HAP, and exclusion if subject to another subpart), and the checklist asks the necessary questions (whether the product is pharmaceutical vs MCPU, presence/use/production of HCl, major-source status, and applicable exemptions). Therefore the key reason in the EPA NOTES is reflected in the criteria provided."}

candidates.title: Site Remediation (Subpart GGGGG)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility at which you conduct a site remediation and that site remediation cleans up a remediation material, is co-located with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP regulated by another 40 CFR part 63 subpart, and your facility is a major source of HAP, then your facility is subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation only cleans up material that does not contain any of the HAP listed in Table 1 of this subpart, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If the total quantity of the HAP listed in Table 1 contained in remediation material excavated, extracted, pumped, or otherwise removed during all site remediations conducted at your facility is less than 1 megagram (Mg) annually, then the site remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart except for the recordkeeping requirement.

If your site remediation is conducted at a gasoline service station to clean up remediation material from a leaking underground storage tank, or at a farm or residential site, or at a qualifying research and development facility under CAA section 112(c)(7), then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If a particular site remediation is completed within 30 consecutive calendar days and meets the initiation, completion, shipment, and documentation conditions in § 63.7884(b), then that site remediation is not subject to the standards in §§ 63.7884 through 63.7887.

If your site remediation includes process vents, remediation material management units, equipment components contacting remediation material that meet the concentration and operating-hour thresholds, or pressure relief devices, then those items are designated affected sources under this subpart.

If the remediation material managed in a remediation material management unit has an average total VOHAP concentration less than 500 ppmw (determined per the referenced procedures), then that remediation material management unit qualifies for the § 63.7886(b)(2) option instead of the controls in § 63.7886(b)(1).

If the remediation material treated or managed by a process vent has an average total VOHAP concentration less than 10 ppmw (determined per the referenced procedures), then that process vent qualifies for the § 63.7885(b)(2) option instead of the controls in § 63.7885(b)(1).

If you designate one or more remediation material management units to be exempted under § 63.7886(d) and the total annual quantity of HAP placed in all designated exempt units is less than 1 Mg/yr and you follow the marking/notification and initial determination requirements, then those units may be exempted from the requirements of § 63.7886(b)(1).

candidates.title: General Provisions (Subpart A)

criteria.criterion: If a source is subject to a relevant standard under this part, then the general provisions in Subpart A (including definitions in § 63.2) apply to that source.

If an affected source is required by a relevant standard to perform performance testing, then the owner or operator must conduct performance tests within the times and under the conditions specified in § 63.7 (unless a waiver or other allowance applies).

If a continuous monitoring system (CMS) or other monitoring is required by a relevant standard, then the owner or operator must comply with the monitoring, operation and maintenance, quality control, and performance-evaluation requirements in § 63.8.

checklist: Determine whether the activity qualifies as "site remediation" (activities that remove, destroy, degrade, transform, immobilize, or otherwise manage remediation material) per the definition in 40 CFR 63.7957.
Determine whether the excavated soil meets the definition of "remediation material" (contains one or more HAP listed in Table 1 of Subpart GGGGG and is soil or similar media) per 40 CFR 63.7957.

Obtain chemical/speciated analysis of the contaminated soil (e.g., Method 305 or other methods) to: (a) identify which HAP from Table 1 are present; (b) calculate VOHAP in ppmw for the soil to assess the <500 ppmw (management-unit option) and <10 ppmw (process-vent option) thresholds; and (c) calculate total mass of HAP in the excavated material to assess the facility-wide 1 Mg/yr threshold.
Calculate the total annual quantity (mass) of the HAP from all site remediations at the facility to determine whether the facility-wide 1 Mg/yr exemption in § 63.7881(c) applies.
Determine whether the facility is a major source of HAP under § 63.2 (potential to emit ≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP).

Identify and document whether the remediation is co-located at the facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition under another Part 63 subpart.

Document the type of units used for temporary storage and management of excavated soil (e.g., containers, open piles, surface impoundments, transfer systems) and whether those units match the affected-source categories in § 63.7882(a).

Determine whether the remediation will be completed within a single 30-consecutive-calendar-day period meeting the conditions of § 63.7884(b) (initiation date, completion/treatment/disposal date, shipment documentation) to evaluate the short-duration exemption.

If claiming any exemption under § 63.7886(d) (exempt units totaling <1 Mg/yr), designate and mark exempt units or prepare the written notification and perform the initial determination and supporting documentation as required.
Check whether the site is an excluded category (gasoline service station UST cleanup, farm or residential site, qualifying R&D) per § 63.7881(b)(4)–(6).

Prepare and retain written documentation supporting all determinations (HAP analyses, VOHAP calculations, mass calculations, exemption determinations, initiation/completion dates), and be prepared to include required notifications/records if you assert an exemption or demonstrate initial compliance per the cited subpart requirements.

If subject to the standard, verify obligations for performance testing and monitoring: readiness to meet § 63.7 performance test timing and § 63.8 monitoring/CMS requirements (develop site-specific plans, QA/QC, and recordkeeping).

The answer requires determining whether the activity qualifies as 'site remediation' and whether material meets the 'remediation material' definition (citing 40 CFR 63.7957 and 63.7881), which encompasses the cleanup requirement cited by EPA. Thus the key rationale from the EPA notes is present."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Organic Liquid Distribution (Non-Gasoline) Operations (OLD)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an organic liquids distribution (OLD) operation that is located at, or is part of, a major source of HAP, then the OLD subpart EEEE applies to that operation (i.e., you are subject to this subpart).
If containers are being loaded or unloaded at transfer racks that are part of an OLD affected source, then those containers while loading/unloading are subject to this subpart.

If the collection of transfer racks at the facility meets the total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume criterion for control in Table 2 (items 7–10), then the transfer racks (and during loading the transport vehicles/containers) are subject to the emission limits and control requirements in §63.2346(b).
citations: 40 CFR 63.2406 (definition of Total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume)

criteria.criterion: If non-permanent containers, transfer racks, transport vehicles, or equipment leak components are used only in special situation distribution loading and unloading operations (such as maintenance or upset liquids management), then those non-permanent items are excluded from the affected source and are not subject to this subpart.

If a pump, valve, or sampling connection operates in organic liquids service for at least 300 hours per year and the affected source has at least one storage tank or transfer rack that meets the applicability criteria in Table 2 or 2b, then equipment leak component requirements (subpart TT/UU/H as referenced) apply under §63.2346(c).

If you are required to submit initial compliance demonstrations or performance tests for emission points subject to this subpart, then you must submit the Notification of Compliance Status and other notifications as required in §63.2382 and the schedules in Table 12 to this subpart.

If an emission source identified in §63.2338 does not require control under §63.2346(a)–(e) (for example because it is below the Table 2 applicability criteria), then that emission source is not required to meet the control provisions but must meet the notification/recordkeeping/reporting requirements for uncontrolled sources in §63.2343.

candidates.title: General Provisions (definitions, performance testing, monitoring)

criteria.criterion: If you are subject to a relevant standard under part 63 (for example subpart EEEE), then the definitions in §63.2 apply for interpreting terms used in that standard.

If the relevant standard (e.g., subpart EEEE) requires performance testing for an emission source, then you must perform the performance test within 180 days of the compliance date (unless a waiver or alternative provision applies).
If the relevant standard requires a continuous monitoring system (CMS) or other monitoring, then the monitoring provisions of §63.8 apply to that CMS as specified in the relevant standard.

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP) (major source determination)?

Do the activities you perform (container-to-container transfers via gravity and non-permanent hoses/valves, and truck-to-container transfers with/without pump) fall within the definition of organic liquids distribution (OLD) operations at your plant site (i.e., storing, transferring, loading/unloading organic liquids)?
Are the transfers conducted at a transfer rack as defined (a single system of loading/unloading arms, hoses, pumps, meters, valves, etc.) or are they isolated, temporary, non-permanent operations?
Are the containers involved 'portable' (drums, totes, portable tanks) or permanent storage tanks (use §63.2406 definition of container and storage tank to classify)?
Are the containers/transfer equipment non-permanent and used only for special-situation distribution (maintenance, upset liquids management) or are they used in routine distribution operations?

What is the total actual annual facility-level organic liquid loading volume through your transfer racks (3-year rolling average) — does it meet or exceed the Table 2 transfer-rack thresholds (items 7–10)?
For transfer rack operations: are transfer racks new or existing (to determine new/source-specific compliance timing)?
Do the transport vehicles or containers have vapor collection equipment or DOT certifications (Method 27/49 CFR part 180) when loading/unloading at your racks?
Do any pumps, valves, or sampling connections operate in organic liquids service ≥300 hours/year (to determine equipment leak component applicability)?

Have you maintained documentation/records required for uncontrolled emission sources (§63.2343) or for controlled sources (records in §63.2390), and prepared notifications (initial notification, Notification of Compliance Status) per §63.2382?
